papers.title: Epitope-conditioned generation of T-cell receptor β-chain CDR3 candidates using a pre-trained transformer model.
papers.abstract: Prioritizing T-cell receptor (TCR) candidates for defined peptide-HLA targets is an important step in TCR-based immunotherapy development, but it still relies heavily on laborious and expensive experimental screening. Recent advancements in generative artificial intelligence have demonstrated promising power in protein design and engineering. In this regard, we propose a pre-trained transformer model, termed Epitope-Receptor-Transformer (ERTransformer), for the epitope-conditioned generation of candidate TCR β-chain CDR3 sequences. ERTransformer is built on EpitopeBERT and ReceptorBERT, which are trained using 1.9 million epitope sequences and 33.1 million TCR sequences, respectively. To demonstrate the model capability, we generate 1,000 candidate TCR β-chain CDR3 sequences for each of the five epitopes with known natural TCRs. The generated candidates show low sequence similarity to natural TCR β-chains while retaining plausible CDR3 length, amino-acid composition, and conservative substitution patterns. We further conduct wet-lab experiments using flow cytometry in defined TCR/pMHC contexts and find that the level of T cell activation induced by selected artificial TCRs is either comparable to or even surpasses that of natural ones. Our work suggests that ERTransformer can expand and prioritize candidate TCR β-chain CDR3 sequences for downstream experimental screening in defined peptide-HLA and TCR-chain contexts.

papers.title: Predicting protein electrostatics with protein language models.
papers.abstract: Ionization states are crucial to protein function, yet predicting their equilibrium constants remains challenging. Here we present KaML-ESMs, sequence-based neural networks built on the ESM protein language models and trained on the GAINES-augmented PKAD-3r dataset. KaML-ESM2/ESMC outperform alternative approaches across four benchmarks, achieving root-mean-square errors of about 0.5 units for Asp/Glu/His/Cys/Tyr/Lys residues in native proteins. Performance degrades on 89 buried engineered mutations lacking evolutionary support, revealing a limitation that supervised training may help overcome. These results suggest that protein sequence, through its evolutionary context, encodes not only structure and function but also, indirectly, electrostatic characteristics. Applying KaML-ESM2 to the entire human proteome, we show that predicted pKa values can identify functional sites and infer catalytic mechanisms. We offer KaML, a sequence-based pKa prediction platform supporting biological exploration, protein engineering, and biomolecular simulation. With further development, GAINES could provide a general framework for addressing data scarcity in machine learning.

papers.title: Leveraging genomic deep learning models for the prediction of noncoding variant effects.
papers.abstract: Characterizing noncoding variant function remains an important challenge in human genetics. Genomic deep learning models have emerged as a promising approach to enable in silico prediction of variant effects. These models include supervised sequence-to-activity models, which predict molecular phenotypes such as genome-wide chromatin states or gene expression levels directly from DNA sequence, and self-supervised genomic language models. Here we review progress in leveraging these models for noncoding variant effect prediction. We describe practical considerations for making such predictions and categorize the types of ground-truth data used to evaluate variant effect predictions, providing insight into the settings in which current models are most useful. Our Review highlights key considerations for practitioners and opportunities for improvement in model development and evaluation.

papers.title: Task-aligned foundation model representations enable single-cell cytokine response inference
papers.abstract: Inferring cellular responses from single-cell transcriptomes requires interpreting changes relative to an appropriate baseline while retaining cell-type context. Here we present CYTAP, which adapts frozen single-cell foundation model embeddings for cytokine-response inference by combining donor-adjusted receiver states with deviations from matched control centroids. CYTAP uses a shared classifier to assign relative single-cell response scores across 90 cytokines and supports unpaired analyses using counterfactual control references. Baseline-relative representations improved held-out-donor prediction with both State SE and scFoundation. Across independent perturbation datasets, CYTAP prioritized applied cytokines, including when receptor transcripts were sparsely detected, and ranked administered cytokines among the top ten in both in vivo datasets. In an unpaired COVID-19 cohort, inferred responses were associated with severity, and IL-6 response scores correlated with plasma IL-6 concentrations. These findings support the use of biologically defined references to adapt pretrained representations for functional response inference.

papers.title: Chromatin-encoded IRX4 identity erosion bounds cardiomyocyte renewal in the infarcted human heart
papers.abstract: Abstract Myocardial infarction leaves the adult human heart unable to regenerate, yet whether injured cardiomyocytes revert to an immature, proliferative state is unresolved. We integrated 1.59 million single-cell and single-nucleus profiles with single-nucleus chromatin accessibility, spatial transcriptomics, plasma-proteome Mendelian randomization and an independent cardiomyopathy cohort of 79 donors to define the injured cardiomyocyte state. Infarcted cardiomyocytes showed a module-wide erosion of ventricular identity, including IRX4, with stress-gene induction and a chromatin-encoded loss of the identity module. Proliferation was not restored: nuclei co-detecting two cell-cycle transcripts remained at 0.011% (5/46,200), and the mitotic signal was confined to the ischaemic core. Genetic dissection separated the identity node from its secretory output: no variant at the IRX4 locus reached genome-wide significance across eight phenotypes, whereas genetically predicted NT-proBNP was causally associated with heart failure (odds ratio 1.12 per standard deviation; 95% confidence interval 1.05-1.19). The ligand and its endothelial receptor NPR1 were spatially uncoupled, and IRX4 erosion did not generalize to chronic cardiomyopathy. The injured cardiomyocyte therefore adopts a chromatin-encoded, non-regenerative stress identity rather than a fetal one, and the natriuretic peptide that reports this state lies on a causal path to heart failure.

papers.title: Virtual Transcriptomics from Routine Histopathology Reveals Metastasis-Associated Programs and Molecular Risk States in Triple-Negative Breast Cancer
papers.abstract: Background: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is a highly aggressive and biologically heterogeneous disease for which reliable biomarkers of metastatic progression remain limited. Although transcriptomic profiling can reveal clinically important molecular programs, its routine implementation is constrained by cost, tissue availability, and workflow complexity. We hypothesized that metastasis-associated transcriptional states are encoded within routine hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) histopathology and can be recovered using artificial intelligence enabled virtual transcriptomics. Methods: We applied the Path2Space foundation model to infer genome-wide gene expression from treatment-naive TNBC H&E tissue microarrays and identified virtual transcriptomic programs associated with lymph node metastasis. We systematically validated candidate genes across three independent international TNBC cohorts (TCGA-BRCA, SCAN-B, and FUSCC). Candidate genes were evaluated in three independent international TNBC cohorts using experimentally measured RNA sequencing, followed by TNBC-specific co-expression network analysis, molecular subtype characterization, and cross-cohort meta-analysis. Results: Virtual transcriptomic analysis nominated 118 candidate genes associated with nodal status at a nominal discovery threshold; these candidates were subsequently evaluated using experimentally measured transcriptomic data across three independent international TNBC cohorts. Cross-cohort validation converged on a parsimonious two-gene Virtual Metastatic Prediction Score (VMPS) composed of TMEM184A and ZNF57, the only genes that remained significantly associated with nodal metastasis across all four datasets. TMEM184A and ZNF57 represented complementary biological programs: a TMEM184A-centered epithelial remodeling network and a ZNF57-centered KRAB zinc-finger transcriptional regulatory network. These transcriptional modules were biologically coherent and demonstrated reproducible associations with established TNBC molecular subtypes. Across TCGA-BRCA, SCAN-B, and FUSCC, the TMEM184A module showed a pooled OR of 1.44 per SD (95% CI, 1.25-1.67; I2=0%), while the two-gene VMPS showed a pooled OR of 1.58 (95% CI, 1.28-1.94). Moreover, higher VMPS and TMEM184A module activity defined reproducible metastatic risk gradients and enriched for lymph node-positive disease across independent cohorts. Conclusions: AI-enabled virtual transcriptomics transforms routine H&E histopathology into a scalable platform for molecular discovery in TNBC. These findings establish virtual transcriptomics as a scalable discovery framework for recovering biologically interpretable, metastasis associated molecular programs from routine histopathology, with potential applications in precision risk stratification.

papers.title: AUTOENCODIX: powering a hub for biological representation learning models
papers.abstract: Autoencoders are a foundational architecture for biological representation learning and empower methods for denoising, multi-modal integration, explainable embeddings, and synthetic data generation. But, new architectures are scattered across isolated repositories, which hampers benchmarking, the reuse of pretrained models, and the transfer to new data modalities. Here, we present the next generation of AUTOENCODIX, a Python package and model hub for biological representation learning. Its modular, standardized API unifies preprocessing, training, hyperparameter optimization, evaluation, generation, and explanation across a growing set of architectures, now including disentangled, masked, semi-supervised, and 2D/3D image autoencoders. To demonstrate its use at scale, we tuned, trained, and benchmarked 15 large autoencoders on a balanced corpus of 3.7 million human cells from CELLxGENE, including nine ontology-based variational autoencoders whose latent dimensions represent core cellular functions and were defined by three large language models (LLMs). The biological-informed embeddings performed on par with classical Principal Component Analysis in downstream classification while being explainable by design, and in synthetic data generation they produced more biologically plausible error profiles than conventional variational autoencoders. Finally, AUTOENCODIX offers a new and unique combination of three pillars of explainability: by-design with biologically-informed latent dimensions, post-hoc gene-to-latent attribution scoring, and LLM-based knowledge integration for verbal description and hypothesis generation. AUTOENCODIX is open-source, open for community extensions and all pretrained models are available via Hugging Face for application on other single-cell gene expression data.

papers.title: Re-timing mortality risk through individualized modelling of lifespan trajectories.
papers.abstract: There is an urgent global need for affordable, large-scale health screening to enhance preventive care in the ageing population. Using low-cost, non-invasive retinal photographs and leveraging large foundation models, we developed a deep learning-based biomarker, Retinal Mortality Equivalent (RetiME), that directly mapped retinal features to individual mortality risk. Trained on a European cohort and externally validated across three independent external cohorts spanning Southeast Asia, Eurasia and North America, RetiME showed robust associations with all-cause and cause-specific mortality and predicted the incidence of a wide range of systemic and ocular diseases. Crucially, beyond static risk estimation, RetiME re-timed mortality risk by reconstructing personalized lifespan trajectories that were associated with observed mortality outcomes (for example, age of death). Clustering of these trajectories revealed distinct mortality patterns, spanning cancer-predominant, cardiometabolic and neurodegenerative risks, reflecting diverse ageing pathways captured by RetiME. Interpretability analyses showed that RetiME captures diverse biological and retinal features underlying mortality risk. Genome-wide analyses further identified genetic loci associated with RetiME. Collectively, these findings support further evaluation of retinal imaging and trajectory modelling as one component of a comprehensive assessment of mortality risk.

papers.title: Multi-omics causal deep learning reveals regulatory structure while interventions refine perturbation predictions
papers.abstract: Inferring gene regulation from single-cell data is difficult because observational measurements cannot distinguish correlation from causation and access to perturbational data, especially with multiple modalities, remains limited. Here we present the Cross-Modal Causal Variational Autoencoder (CMC-VAE), which learns a network linking genes and proteins (gene-gene, protein-protein and gene-protein) in the latent space and maps each connection back onto measured features. Trained on 809,130 observational CITE-seq profiles, CMC-VAE recovers co-expression, transcription factor regulons and immune signalling programs, and learns a sparse cross-modal map enriched for transcript-protein cognate pairs. On three CRISPR screens used during development, it ranks knockout-responsive genes better than correlation and latent-VAE baselines. Fitted to a screen's unperturbed control cells, without perturbation labels, the model translates measured knockout RNA responses into protein responses better than a correlation map and cognate transcripts. The direction of gene-to-gene regulation, however, is not recovered from observational data. On the CITE-seq screens, fine-tuning only the latent network improves held-out response correlation, mainly by learning a response shared across knockouts. On larger Perturb-seq screens, with about 1,000 training perturbations, fine-tuning the latent network learns gene-specific effects that transfer to held-out genes, more so than a gene-level causal model fine-tuned on the same cells, and in simulation, such interventions also restore edge orientations that observational training leaves unresolved.

papers.title: An interpretable framework for decoding transcriptomic foundation models
papers.abstract: Transcriptomic foundation models are pretrained on millions of single-cell profiles, but what their hidden states encode, and whether it holds on targeted spatial panels, is uncertain. We present interpreTFM, a layer-resolved framework that extracts frozen activations from scGPT, Geneformer, and C2S-scale, decomposes each evaluated layer with a sparse autoencoder (SAE), and evaluates the resulting features against raw hidden dimensions, an untrained SAE of the same width, and single genes, holding out either gene-token rows or whole genes. Concept-associated features are then projected to cells for spatial niche discovery and interface analysis. We applied the framework to a CosMx lung-cancer section (81,236 cells, 960 genes) and a Xenium renal-cell-carcinoma section (465,220 cells, 399 model-compatible genes), screening 29 model-layer combinations per dataset. On held-out observations of known genes, sparse features marked 262--593 biological concepts per analysis layer, against 0--70 for raw hidden dimensions and 0--249 for the untrained SAE; on genes held out during feature selection, concept F1 was 0.01--0.12 for every representation and lowest for sparse features, so a feature's concept label reflects the genes it detects, and randomly re-initialized models scored the same. A linear readout of the hidden states recovered the concept membership of unseen genes (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve 0.66--0.75, versus 0.59--0.61 for co-expression and cell-type profiles, and chance level for randomly re-initialized scGPT and Geneformer), so this information is learned and distributed across dimensions. At the cell level, sparse features were about twice as population-specific as raw hidden dimensions and approached single marker genes, and this held in four further CosMx donors. In the analyzed CosMx section, niches built from sparse features agreed with author cell types more closely than label-composition and expression-only niches and converged across models; in the further donors their concept-level definition recurred, whereas their composition did not. In the single Xenium section, three of five niches per model (lymphoid, tumor/myeloid, tumor/vascular) were shared across models and also emerged from measured expression alone. A macrophage's sparse profile predicted the myeloid composition of its neighborhood about as well as the full gene panel, also in three further donors. Within model niches, ligand--receptor co-localization recurred directionally across CosMx donors and placed CCL19--CCR7 in the Xenium lymphoid niche, whereas the models' own interface calls, under a local, stratified null with a threshold calibrated on contact-free fields, were at chance level in CosMx and tracked transcript spillover in Xenium. interpreTFM thus provides held-out tests that separate gene detection from concept generalization, and features that make cells and niches comparable across models and patients while carrying the information

papers.title: GASTON-VI efficiently quantifies spatial axes and molecular gradients from multi-sample, multi-modal spatial-omics data
papers.abstract: Many tissues exhibit an underlying spatial axis along which fundamental biological processes occur due to continuous spatial gradients of cell type and molecular state. Modern spatial-omics technologies measure molecular features (e.g. gene/protein expression) at 100,000s-1,000,000s of locations within a two-dimensional (2-D) tissue slice, with large-scale atlases profiling multiple tissue slices of the same organ type across different individuals and biological conditions (e.g. healthy versus diseased). However, existing computational methods for identifying spatial molecular gradients are limited to small spatial transcriptomics datasets (1000s of cells) of a single tissue slice, while methods for integrating multiple samples do not explicitly model spatial axes nor spatial molecular gradients along such axes. Here, we present GASTON-VI, a variational inference (VI)-based deep learning model which efficiently learns an underlying spatial axis and spatial molecular gradients along this axis from multi-sample, multi-condition spatial-omics data of any molecular modality (e.g. transcriptomics, proteomics). GASTON-VI jointly learns (1) a spatial coordinate (the "isodepth") for each individual tissue slice and (2) 1-D spatial modality functions that describe molecular gradients along the isodepth for tissues of the same biological condition, while utilizing a latent variable model to account for batch effects. Further, GASTON-VI implements a statistical test for identifying molecules with differential spatial gradients across biological conditions (e.g. healthy versus diseased). On spatial transcriptomics and proteomics data from the intestine, tonsil, and liver, we show that GASTON-VI recovers spatial axes and molecular gradients along these axes more accurately and efficiently than existing methods. In particular, applied to large-scale spatial transcriptomics and proteomics atlases, GASTON-VI reveals differential spatial gradients of gene expression along the portal vein-central vein axis in fibrotic livers, and differential spatial gradients of protein abundance along the muscularis-lumen axis across different regions of the intestine. Software availability: GASTON-VI is available at https://github.com/chitra-lab/GASTON-VI.

papers.title: Model evaluation metrics of Virtual Cell Challenge 2026
papers.abstract: Virtual cell models aim to predict the effects of genetic, environmental, chemical and other perturbations in silico, reducing the dependency on complex and costly experiments. The Virtual Cell Challenge 2026 motivates the field toward this goal, tasking models with zero-shot prediction of the transcriptional responses to CRISPRi knockdowns in six human cell lines. The faithfulness of a model to the experiment is assessed by metrics that compare its predictions with the real data, and designing such metrics is not trivial. We developed the metrics of the 2026 Challenge around three principles: a metric should (i) reflect the biological information extracted from experiments, (ii) be calibrated on a repeat of the experiment, and (iii) resist shortcut solutions that raise the score without predicting the response. Here we present the six resulting metrics, the reasoning behind each of them, and their evaluations on the Challenge data. Two of the metrics compare the pseudobulk expression profiles of predicted and measured cells, while four assess the genes that respond to each perturbation, the central readout of a Perturb-seq experiment. The metrics are implemented in cell-eval2, an open-source Python package. On the Challenge data, all six metrics score a repeat of the experiment above the mean baseline, and the shortcut solutions that the metrics of the 2025 Challenge left open can no longer raise the score. The new metrics are therefore more robust than the previous ones.

papers.title: Integrating CRISPRi perturbation responses and transcription-factor binding priors for regulatory network inference in triple-negative breast cancer
papers.abstract: Triple-Negative Breast Cancer (TNBC) represents an aggressive breast cancer subtype that lacks actionable cell-surface receptors, restricting frontline systemic management to cytotoxic chemotherapy. While recent functional epigenomics shows that TNBC progression is governed by non-coding regulatory remodeling at distal super-enhancers, conventional Gene Regulatory Network (GRN) inference methods rely on observational transcriptomic co-expression, which suffers from technical dropouts and confounding correlations that inflate false discoveries (>30%). Here, we present an interventional network inference framework that integrates large-scale single-cell CRISPR-interference perturbation sequencing (Perturb-seq; GSE224986, 95,678 cells across 11,975 sgRNAs) with ENCODE Factorbook ChIP-seq physical transcription factor binding priors across 819 somatic mutation-associated enhancer loci in human TNBC (MDA-MB-231). Our pipeline reconstructed a tripartite network yielding 5,935 physical TF-enhancer edges, 383,757 functional enhancer-gene edges, and 542,760 unique TF-target gene functional pairs across 372 active enhancers. Topological centrality prioritized master transcriptional drivers governing TNBC oncogenic signaling, including CTCF, POLR2A, EP300, JUND, MYC, and FOS, which regulate Hallmark programs for Epithelial-Mesenchymal Transition (p = 1.2 x 10-9) and cell cycle progression. Explainable machine learning (SHAP TreeExplainer) revealed non-linear, thresholded transactivation dynamics for AP-1 and MYC. Quantitative benchmarking against held-out CRISPRi ground truth demonstrated strong discriminatory accuracy (AUROC = 0.8999, AUPRC = 0.8745, Precision = 90.13%, FDR = 9.87%), substantially outperforming GENIE3 (AUPRC = 0.6323, FDR = 35.73%) and co-expression correlation (AUPRC = 0.6814). In silico-simulated driver feature silencing correlated with experimental responses (R2 = 0.473, p < 10-122), and master driver signatures significantly stratified overall survival in the METABRIC (n = 320) and TCGA-BRCA (n = 160; p [≤] 0.019) cohorts. Finally, in silico perturbation modeling indicated that multi-target epigenetic combinations achieved 93% topological disruption of oncogenic regulatory connectivity, nominating prioritized candidate circuits for experimental validation.

papers.title: LitGene: an interpretable transformer model integrating text and ontology for gene representation learning.
papers.abstract: Representation learning in genomics often relies on sequence, expression, and network data, thereby overlooking a wealth of insights in the scientific literature. Here, we present LitGene, an interpretable transformer-based model that refines gene representations by integrating unstructured textual information with Gene Ontology annotations through contrastive learning. In evaluations across eight benchmark tasks for protein properties, LitGene achieves competitive accuracy and exhibits zero-shot prediction of GO terms, KEGG pathways, and gene-disease associations. LitGene identified ANGPTL6 as a potential candidate gene for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF), supported by its differential expression in independent IPF samples, illustrating LitGene's utility for hypothesis generation. A SHAP-based interpretability tool highlights text features influencing predictions, while an automated literature-grounding framework provides corroborating support where available. Our results suggest that integrating textual and genetic information may help reduce biases associated with under-studied genes. The model is released as open-source code, along with a publicly accessible web interface at https://litgene.cs.unm.edu/ , which allows users to submit gene names, disease names, drug names, or custom text (e.g., publication abstracts) to obtain evidence-based predictions of related biomedical entities.

papers.title: BioGCD: A Biology-Guided Multimodal Framework for Compound and Combination Discovery
papers.abstract: Phenotype-based transcriptomic screening provides a powerful approach for therapeutic discovery by capturing how compounds reshape cellular states. However, existing perturbation models lack biological constraints, limiting generalizability, mechanistic interpretability, and the ability to prioritize experimentally validated candidates. Here, we developed BioGCD, a biological knowledge-guided multimodal framework that integrates four gene-level prior graphs and a compound-aware pathway-level prior with cellular states, molecular structures and dosage information to learn biologically informed perturbation patterns. BioGCD outperformed existing models in predicting compound induced transcriptomic responses across diverse cellular contexts, achieving a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.912 between predicted and observed responses. Beyond prediction, the model enabled mechanistic interpretation of compounds effects by attributing predicted activities to specific molecular substructures and inferring potential pathways associated with compound responses. The proportion of the top 30 candidates supported by literature evidence or experimental validation varied across cell lines, reaching 70% in a melanoma cell line and a liver cancer cell line, and 30% in a breast cancer cell line. For previously uncharacterized agents, experimental screening of the top 50 candidates identified Z6412951658 as an anti-melanoma hit. Moreover, the BioGCD prediction-based model correctly classified 8 of 10 randomly selected compound combinations as synergistic or non-synergistic in melanoma cells. Overall, BioGCD establishes a biologically grounded AI framework for learning generalizable perturbation representations, enabling systematic therapeutic discovery through accurate prediction and biological insight.

papers.title: Do single-cell foundation models need 512 dimensions for one number?
papers.abstract: Single-cell foundation models represent counts through high-dimensional value embeddings or ranked feature tokens. We asked how many dimensions counts need and what network computes. In a controlled Transformer, a four-dimensional value track separated from a wide gene-identity backbone retains nearly all masked-prediction net gain; a straight line replaces pretrained value curves with little transfer loss. Across evaluated cohorts, clamping detected-gene values retains most gain in annotation, surface-protein prediction and perturbation-shift consistency, consistent with the prevalence of single-molecule counts. A two-feature encoder combining tie-free rank and within-cell standardized magnitude improves controlled retraining and preserves annotation when grafted onto pretrained scGPT. Gene offsets and three linear cell-level scalars approximate masked prediction and predict responses to count thinning; depth leads in the controlled model, while cell type leads in scGPT. Matched controls show that attribution, attention, dictionary and probe readouts can reflect depth, gene frequency, hub degree or directions that transfer little output.

papers.title: General-purpose language models are neurosymbolic reasoners able to annotate proteins from sequence
papers.abstract: Determining the function of genes across the tree of life is one of the major challenges in biology. Generative AI approaches to this problem generally fall into two categories: language models trained on biological sequences that are able to predict structure and function from signals in those sequences; and generalist language models trained on text, that are able to reason about biological function symbolically. A default operating assumption is that protein language models do not perform well on symbolic tasks, and that generalist language models do not perform well on sequence tasks. However, a recent report showed that frontier generalist models perform surprisingly well on next-residue prediction tasks. We set out to explore whether these capabilities extended to protein annotation. We assigned different frontier generalist models a variety of protein annotation tasks, including predicting the presence and coordinates of Pfam domains, loss of functional catalytic residues, and predicting structure and activity. On all annotation tasks, the frontier models performed well above chance; we did not benchmark them against specialised tools. The models also make characteristic hallucination errors, and they state them as confidently as their correct calls. Though untested against specialised methods, the nascent ability of frontier models to perform protein annotation from sequence alone is intriguing. The ability to reason over sequence, structure, and symbols in a single model allows for a neurosymbolic approach where a combination of sequence, experimental data and knowledge from the literature can be holistically combined to improve on de novo functional annotation of the protein universe. Prompts, test sets, model outputs and code: https://github.com/ai4curation/fable-sequence-to-function. Summary of results: https://ai4curation.io/fable-sequence-to-function/

papers.title: ARCADE: Controllable Codon Design from Foundation Models via Activation Engineering.
papers.abstract: Coding sequence design requires optimizing multiple biological properties, which may be either aligned or in trade-off, and are typically measured as continuous-valued metrics. However, existing codon design methods lack explicit control over these objectives. Moreover, current controllable generation techniques are largely developed for discrete, human-interpretable attributes, leaving a gap in controllably steering continuous biological properties in genomic sequence design. We introduce ARCADE (Activation engineeRing for ControllAble coDon dEsign), a machine learning framework for flexible and controllable multi-objective codon design. ARCADE leverages pretrained genomic language models and extends activation engineering from discrete attribute control to continuous-valued biological metrics. By deriving biologically meaningful semantic steering vectors in the model's activation space, ARCADE enables direct control over properties such as Codon Adaptation Index, minimum free energy, GC content, as well as their combinations. Comprehensive evaluations demonstrate that ARCADE supports robust single- and multi-objective steering, enabling simultaneous modulation of multiple properties without retraining model parameters. Source code for the method and to reproduce the results is available at https://github.com/Kingsford-Group/arcade and archived on Zenodo (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.21140668). Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.

papers.title: OpenDVP: an experimental and computational framework for community-empowered deep visual proteomics.
papers.abstract: Deep visual proteomics (DVP) is an emerging approach for cell-type-specific and spatially resolved proteomics. However, its broad adoption has been constrained by the lack of an open-source end-to-end workflow within a community-driven ecosystem. Here we introduce openDVP, an experimental and computational framework for accessible and scalable DVP. OpenDVP combines open-source image analysis tools (MCMICRO, QuPath and napari) with scverse formats (AnnData and SpatialData) for multiomics integration. It provides two workflows: a fast-track pipeline requiring no image analysis expertise, and an artificial intelligence-powered pipeline incorporating state-of-the-art methods for image preprocessing, segmentation and spatial analysis. We apply openDVP across three archival tissue studies (human placenta, early stage lung cancer and locally relapsed breast cancer), integrating spatial single-cell phenotypes with exploratory proteomic measurements. Finally, we introduce deep proteomic profiling of cellular neighborhoods as a scalable approach for spatial discovery proteomics.

papers.title: Evaluating generative models for structure-based drug discovery from de novo design to lead optimization.
papers.abstract: Advances in protein structure prediction have created opportunities for structure-based drug design, yet translating structural knowledge into actionable small-molecule ligands remains difficult. Existing benchmarks often use simplified datasets and computational surrogates that poorly capture the heterogeneity and constraints of real-world drug discovery. We introduce MolGenBench, a comprehensive benchmark for de novo molecular generation and hit-to-lead optimization built on a large, structurally diverse dataset. Evaluation of 17 leading methods reveals persistent limitations, including weak virtual-screening performance, limited coverage of target-specific bioactive space, frequent high-risk structural motifs, poor target awareness, and reduced generalization to unseen proteins. Although some models improve three-dimensional conformation generation, they still struggle to produce active molecules reliably. MolGenBench provides standardized data, metrics, and analyses that connect structural prediction with practical molecular design and guide the development of more effective structure-based generative models.

papers.title: TW-GMProt: Trust-Weighted Semi-Supervised Gated Modulation Protein Language Model for Antimicrobial Peptide Activity Prediction
papers.abstract: Antibiotic resistance poses a major global health threat, underscoring the need for faster approaches to antimicrobial discovery. Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) are promising therapeutic candidates, but experimental activity screening remains costly and time-consuming. We introduce TW-GMProt, a trust-weighted semi-supervised gated modulation protein language model for quantitative AMP activity prediction. It integrates pretrained protein language model representations with convolutional neural networks through a gated modulation strategy, complemented by biophysical priors. To address the scarcity of experimental data, the framework further employs trust-weighted semi-supervised learning to leverage a large collection of unlabeled antimicrobial peptides through pseudo-labeling. For minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) prediction against Escherichia coli, TW-GMProt achieved an RMSE of 0.434, Kendalls{tau} of 0.582, R2 of 0.622, and Pearsons r of 0.792. Compared with MSCMamba, these results correspond to a significant reduction of over 17% lower RMSE (p = 1.95 x 10-3), over 25% higher Kendalls{tau} , over 30% higher R2, and more than 15% higher Pearson correlation. Comparable predictive performance was observed for Staphylococcus aureus, supporting the applicability of the framework across Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria. These results demonstrate that combining gated multimodal representation learning with trust-weighted semi-supervised training provides an effective strategy for AMP activity prediction.

papers.title: GinsengMind: An evidence-grounded AI research agent for integrative molecular research in Panax ginseng
papers.abstract: Panax ginseng C. A. Meyer is one of the most extensively studied medicinal plants, with substantial pharmaceutical and economic importance owing to its diverse bioactive constituents, particularly ginsenosides. Despite considerable advances in ginseng molecular research, the fragmentation of genomic, transcriptomic, protein structural, and biochemical information remains a major challenge for investigating gene function and specialized metabolism. Here, we developed GinsengMind (https://ginsengai.nrc.ac.cn), an evidence-grounded AI research agent that integrates species-specific molecular knowledge with large language model (LLM)-guided tool orchestration and structured retrieval-augmented generation. Built upon the telomere-to-telomere reference genome of P. ginseng, GinsengMind integrates 77,266 genes, 154,754 transcripts, and 77,266 protein records. Comprehensive functional annotation using Swiss-Prot, eggNOG, and InterProScan covered 97.00% of the 76,947 quality-controlled proteins. The platform further incorporates 71,046 ESMFold-predicted protein structures, 7,263,004 gene expression records across 94 RNA-seq samples, and 4,813 bibliographic records. Six specialized research tools enable autonomous evidence retrieval and source-linked scientific interpretation through natural-language interaction. To evaluate its performance, we established GinsengBench, comprising 50 curated questions across six research categories. In a blinded evaluation by three experts, GinsengMind achieved a mean weighted composite score of 96.18 across ten core questions, substantially exceeding GLM-5.3 without database access (23.24; mean paired difference, 72.94; 95% confidence interval, 65.19-79.87). Across five shared questions, GinsengMind outperformed nine general-purpose LLMs on average and achieved a score (96.56) close to that of GLM-5.3 supplied with predefined evidence packages (96.88), highlighting the importance of domain-specific knowledge and autonomous evidence retrieval. A case study of the ginsenoside biosynthetic enzyme PgUGT94Q2 further illustrates how integrated molecular evidence can reveal unresolved biological relationships and identify priorities for subsequent experimental investigation. Beyond conventional database querying, GinsengMind provides a foundation for exploring potential biological associations, prioritizing candidate biosynthetic genes, and formulating experimentally testable hypotheses. We anticipate that GinsengMind will facilitate research on medicinal plant specialized metabolism, natural product biosynthesis, enzyme discovery and engineering, and synthetic biology, while offering an adaptable framework for developing domain-specialized AI research agents across other medicinal plants and scientific disciplines.

papers.title: Circuit-aligned specialization of human basal ganglia astrocytes.
papers.abstract: Astrocytes shape synapses and circuits, yet their diversity within the human basal ganglia remains poorly defined. Integrating single-nucleus transcriptomic and epigenomic profiling with spatial transcriptomics, we identify three anatomically organized astrocyte subgroups-striatal gray matter (GM), extra-striatal GM, and white matter (WM)-distinguished by neurotransmitter transporter expression and synapse-associated programs that reflect afferent input. These molecular distinctions generalize brain-wide, separating telencephalic from non-telencephalic astrocytes, with LHX2 marking telencephalic astrocyte identity across species. Within the striatum (STR), dorsal and ventral populations align with distinct microcircuits; a ventral population maps to the nucleus accumbens mediodorsal shell alongside specialized neuronal subtypes, a pattern conserved in nonhuman primates. A deep learning sequence model identifies subgroup-specific enhancer codes and recovers established transcription factor motif logic from published enhancer-AAV datasets, providing a foundation for targeted viral vector design. These findings define intersecting axes of human astrocyte specialization and offer a framework for cell-type-specific dissection of basal ganglia circuits.

papers.title: GATA transcription factors coordinate developmental progression in the arabidopsis root.
papers.abstract: Proper organ development requires the coordination of cell type-specific differentiation programs with general maturation processes through precise spatiotemporal gene regulation. In plants, where RNA polymerase pausing is not well established, alternative mechanisms must ensure this coordination. Here, using single-cell resolution transcriptomic and chromatin accessibility data, we reconstruct developmental trajectories of the Arabidopsis root ground tissue to investigate these mechanisms. We describe phased transcriptional landscapes governing the transition from stem cell to early differentiation, in which chromatin accessibility marks the activation of key developmental regulators. A major transcriptional switch in the late meristematic zone, underpinned by extensive chromatin remodeling, drives the transition from cell division to differentiation. Leveraging machine learning to examine integrated transcriptomic and chromatin accessibility trajectories, we identify GATA transcription factors (TFs) as central coordinators of this switch; a role we validate experimentally. We show that the GATA TFs sit at the tipping point of a feedback-driven bistable system that integrates inputs from auxin and cytokinin to balance proliferation and differentiation, ensuring temporal precision in root development at both the tissue and organ scales.

papers.title: Heterogeneity co-evolves with architecture to determine colon cancer outcome.
papers.abstract: Intratumoural heterogeneity, originating from genetic, epigenetic and phenotypic diversity, is pervasive in cancer and a fundamental barrier to curative treatment1,2. How these heterogeneous cell states emerge and co-evolve within tumours remains poorly understood. Here we develop a deep-learning framework that quantifies colorectal cancer tissue architecture and nuclear morphology at subcellular resolution to predict patient outcome. Integrating this with spatial transcriptomics, multiplex immunofluorescence and patient-derived organoids, we identify a co-evolutionary relationship between tumour architecture and cancer cell states. We identify architectural interfaces in colorectal cancer that drive cell state diversification by promoting distinct cancer stem cell programmes. Specifically, tissue fragmentation generates compressive forces that activate YAP, suppressing classical stem cell programmes and inducing fetal/regenerative stem cell states that initially manifest as hybrid states with features of partial epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT). Subsequent tumour-stroma communication through TGFβ diversifies these into distinct stem cell and EMT states. Reciprocally, β-catenin activity tunes tumour cell responsiveness to architectural cues. Collectively, this work identifies a feedforward loop between cell states and tissue architecture that drives cancer heterogeneity and cell state diversification. Machine-learning-based analyses harness this co-dependency, independently of mutational status or cancer stage, to predict patient outcome.

papers.title: HoloGene: Learning to Lift Sliced Spatial Transcriptomics to Holistic 3D Gene Fields
papers.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) provides spatially resolved gene expression measurements, but most 3D ST datasets are acquired as independently processed 2D sections. Computational approaches span slice registration and integration, explicit or generative interpolation, and coordinate-field modeling. Within the last family, implicit neural representations (INRs) offer a continuous, coordinate-queryable parameterization, but standard isotropic coordinate encodings do not explicitly reflect that serial-section measurements are dense in-plane and sparse along the axial direction. We present HoloGene, an anisotropic conditional INR framework for estimating continuous 3D gene-expression fields from pre-registered ST sections. Its central contribution is an acquisition-aware factorization that couples dense in-plane synthesis with sparse axial evolution using established GAE, FiLM, pseudo-label supervision, and CORAL components. HoloGene compresses high-dimensional expression profiles into a graph-autoencoder latent manifold, uses pseudo-label-derived signature conditioning to provide coarse intra-section context, and applies depth-dependent FiLM modulation to model axial variation. A signature-stratified correlation-alignment regularizer encourages cross-slice covariance alignment in latent features. Using held-out measured sections as cross-sectional references, HoloGene improves reconstruction accuracy and biological preservation metrics compared with general-purpose INRs and adapted spatial-transcriptomics baselines. These results support anisotropic conditional modeling as a practical strategy for estimating 3D expression fields from discontinuous ST sections. Code is available at https://github.com/Szym29/HoloGene.

papers.title: A gene informed benchmark for BioScoring of pathology foundation models
papers.abstract: Pathology foundation models are usually compared by their performance on downstream tasks such as classification and retrieval. While such benchmarks measure how useful a model is, they provide no insight into the biology it represents. We introduce BioScore, a benchmark that quantifies how well an image encoder captures cell identities, with spatial transcriptomics of the same tissue as the reference. A sparse autoencoder splits the encoder's patch embeddings into sparse features, which we cluster into a fixed number of groups. BioScore then measures, for each of 52 cell identities defined by marker genes, how specifically one group follows the identity's expression over the tissue. Because the autoencoder training is fully unsupervised, a match shows that the model represents the cell identity from the image alone. We score 8 pathology foundation models and 3 natural-image models. Every pathology model scores above every natural-image model (0.299--0.371 \vs 0.214--0.232), and paired tests separate three tiers among the pathology models. Unlike a supervised probe, BioScore needs no labels, builds its reference from the data and scores even from few sections, yet it ranks the encoders as a probe does. Its per-identity breakdown indicates which cell identities each encoder captures or misses.

papers.title: Weight locking as a safeguard for open-weight biological foundation models
papers.abstract: Biological foundation models can accelerate research, but their open weight release raises biosecurity concerns. A common safeguard excludes eukaryotic viral genomes from training, but fine-tuning on public viral data reverses it. We confirm that fine-tuning improves held-out viral language modelling, and that the gain comes from the viral data itself. Weight locking by spectral deformation, proposed to prevent fine-tuning, is untested in biological models. We applied it to two Evo-family models and the protein model ESM3-open, against attackers of increasing knowledge. The lock defends against the naive attacker, whose fine-tuning drives capability below pretrained on all three models. It does not defend against an informed attacker, who freezes or fuses the compensation matrix to restore near-unlocked performance. A compensation-free lock we build from the network's own rescaling symmetries again defeats the naive attacker, but canonical rebalancing removes it without knowledge of the lock. The barrier is one of knowledge, not compute.

papers.title: XenoType: Decoding cellular identity in breast cancer histology through molecular supervision
papers.abstract: Characterizing the cellular composition of the tumor microenvironment from histological images is fundamental to understanding cancer biology and informing treatment decisions. Deep learning has enabled automated nuclear detection and classification from hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) images, yet cell classifiers remain largely confined to broad morphological categories owing to a reliance on manual annotations. Recent efforts have used spatial molecular measurements to supervise histological classification, but these approaches often require separate tissue sections or produce altered H&E staining, and the resulting cell-type annotations depend on subjective choices such as marker selection and clustering parameters. Here we develop XenoType, a framework that classifies cells into seven molecularly informed categories directly from routine histology, trained using paired same-section Xenium spatial transcriptomics. Cell-type annotations are reconciled from four single-cell RNA-sequencing references, reducing dependence on marker choices. Across eight held-out breast tissue sections, XenoType outperformed commonly used CellViT++ retrained on the same molecular annotations under both four-class (macro-F1: 0.703 vs. 0.569) and seven-class (macro-F1: 0.571 vs. 0.403) taxonomies, with the largest gains for myoepithelial (F1: 0.175 to 0.572) and endothelial cells (F1: 0.395 to 0.682). Molecular measurements are required only during training; at inference, XenoType uses the H&E image alone. Model-reference agreement increased consistently with annotation confidence, and XenoType generalized to an independently profiled breast tissue section from a different spatial transcriptomics platform, supporting scalable cell-type mapping from routine histology without per-specimen molecular profiling.

papers.title: Vir2vec: A Genome-Wide Viral Embedding
papers.abstract: Genomic language models (gLMs) enable the extraction of meaningful numerical representations from DNA sequences, yet existing approaches primarily focus on human genomes or limited viral datasets, and systematic evaluations of viral representations remain scarce. Here, we introduce Vir2vec, a family of decoder-only gLMs (from 17M to 422M parameters) continually pretrained on a curated viral corpus comprising 565,747 complete genomes and genomic segment records assigned to 295 different species. We also present the viral Genome Understanding Evaluation (vGUE), a seven-task evaluation suite assessing viral representations across broad organism discrimination, evolutionary signatures, intra-genus species classification, variant subtyping, and host-associated phenotypes. Evaluated as a frozen feature extractor under nested cross-validation, Vir2vec achieves the highest balanced accuracy on three of seven tasks (full-genome virus detection, DNA-versus-RNA classification, and host-category prediction) and shares the highest performance on HIV-1 versus HIV-2 classification, while alternative models lead on the remaining three tasks. Taxonomic exclusion experiments further assess generalization of classification capabilities when an RNA-virus clade is excluded from pretraining at species and family levels. Finally, we introduce an argmax-routed SHAP explainability framework that maps feature attributions to codon-level sequence coordinates, highlighting receptor-binding-domain positions associated with SARS-CoV-2 human-versus-mouse host specificity discrimination. Together, Vir2vec and vGUE provide resources for advancing viral genomic representation learning and its systematic evaluation.

papers.title: FiberTron enables regulatory variant effect prediction and testing from multi-omic long reads of a single sample
papers.abstract: State-of-the-art sequence-to-function models are trained on large compendia of public data to predict regulatory activity across hundreds of cell types. However, they are not designed to interpret individual genomes, effects in under-sampled cell types, or provide a comprehensive view of how genetic variation influences complex diseases. Here we show that a single sample profiled with Fiber-seq and Nanopore direct RNA-seq contains enough information to train such a model from scratch. FiberTron, a 12M parameter convolutional-transformer model, takes 524 kb of reference sequence and predicts CpG methylation, chromatin accessibility and strand-specific transcript coverage at base-pair resolution (median Pearson's r of 0.85-0.97 on held-out chromosomes). Trained in under a day on a single four-GPU node, our HG002 model performs on par with models such as AlphaGenome on dsQTL and eQTL variant effect prediction tasks, despite being over an order of magnitude smaller. As training uses reference sequence only, each sample's phased multi-omic long reads remain available to test its variant-effect predictions. FiberTron recapitulates OAS1 splicing variation associated with COVID-19 risk, recovers 79% of allele-specific accessibility variants in a melanoma line, identifies oncogenic TERT promoter and TAL1 enhancer mutations, and predicts EWSR1::ATF1 fusion transcript expression and its unique chromatin imprint in a rare clear cell sarcoma patient sample. Lightweight single-sample training brings base-resolution interpretation of non-coding variation within reach of individual laboratories.

papers.title: A multimodal foundation model for tissue proteomics and morphology in cancer
papers.abstract: Cancer diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment decisions increasingly rely on integrating tissue morphology with specific molecular readouts of the tumor and its microenvironment. H&E histopathology provides scalable morphology, whereas multiplex spatial proteomics quantifies dozens of proteins in situ with spatial context, but remains selectively deployed, often with different marker panels across cohorts. This creates a translational bottleneck: most patients lack high-depth molecular profiling, and existing models rarely integrate morphology and spatial molecular data in a single framework. We present VirTues-M2, a multimodal foundation model that jointly learns from H&E and spatial proteomics using a novel vision transformer-based architecture. By encoding marker identity during pretraining, VirTues-M2 is robust to missing modalities, imperfect modality pairing or registration, and variable marker panels, enabling unified inference for tissue phenotyping, panoptic cell segmentation, virtual staining, annotation-free biomarker discovery, and reinforcement learning-based adaptive marker panel selection to reduce assay burden. As a concrete demonstration of translational utility, in a newly collected cohort of 1,053 treatment-naive non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) patients with paired spatial proteomics and H&E, VirTues-M2 discovers high-risk and low-risk tissue signatures that stratify overall survival in both the discovery cohort and an independent validation cohort, outperforming current state-of-the-art stratification schemes; all enabled by VirTues-M2's ability to jointly analyze both modalities within a single model.

papers.title: LeCellModel: Interpretable Density Estimation over the Gene Expression Manifold
papers.abstract: Representation learning for single-cell RNA-seq has been evaluated by the identities representations capture -- cell types, lineages, perturbations -- rather than how faithfully they model the distribution of cell states on the gene expression manifold. As a result, density estimation, rare-state detection, perturbation scoring, and gene-level attribution are bolted onto frozen embeddings as separate models, disconnected from the geometry of the data. We argue that modeling the distribution of cell states should be the primary objective, and that representation quality follows from it. Building on LeJEPA, whose SIGReg objective enforces a provably optimal isotropic Gaussian latent, we introduce LeCellModel, which reads the encoder's Jacobian log-volume (JEPA-SCORE) under this Gaussian latent as a relative typicality score. Across several datasets, LeCellModel outperforms established methods on the scIB benchmark for representation quality. Furthermore, we show that LeCellModel enables detection of rare expression states using JEPA-SCORE as a typicality measure, applying it to a controlled cytokine panel, where it identifies stimulated cells across minority fractions and tracks pathway-response magnitude. We introduce gene-level interpretability of the typicality score -- to our knowledge, the first method for analyzing JEPA-SCORE in feature space. Leveraging this framework, LeCellModel recapitulates the known association of a profibrotic macrophage program with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, and discovers a CD177+ activated regulatory T cell subpopulation previously described only in tumor contexts. Both findings emerge directly from the geometry of the learned embedding, without relying on supervised annotations.

papers.title: GABIF: An Adaptive Guided Graph Denoising Framework for Antibody Conditional Inverse Folding
papers.abstract: Antibodies play a central role in the human immune system, and their design is critical for vaccine development, therapeutic intervention, and improving human longevity. However, the vast combinatorial search space of antibodies poses a fundamental challenge for de novo discovery. Recent advances in deep learning, particularly denoising diffusion models, have demonstrated strong potential in protein inverse folding. Nevertheless, existing approaches are largely constrained to learning from natural antibody repertoires, thereby generating sequences that closely resemble natural antibodies. Such similarity, however, does not necessarily translate into improved functional performance in downstream applications. In this work, we develop a novel generative protein design model that enables the generation and optimization of antibody sequences tailored to specific downstream tasks and target metrics. Besides training on given an antibody dataset, we guide the generative model by an antibody-antigen binding affinity predictor for conditional discrete diffusion. The model is pre-trained on a given antibody dataset. Meanwhile, an antibody-antigen binding affinity predictor is incorporated as a conditional signal in a discrete diffusion framework, where a regressor serves as the conditional probability to guide the learning of the amino acid probability distribution of sequences under the objective of affinity optimization. In silico experiments demonstrate that our antibody design model achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art approaches, while the proposed regressor effectively improves binding affinity, as validated by an independent external predictor. Furthermore, our results highlight that the combination of finetuning and supervised guidance provides a powerful paradigm for adapting pretrained models to downstream tasks.

papers.title: An open long non-coding RNA foundation model for generalizable prediction
papers.abstract: Long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) play essential roles in transcriptional regulation and chromatin organization, yet predicting their functional properties from sequence remains challenging because informative signals span both local motifs and long-range base pairing across kilobase-scale transcripts. Current RNA foundation models are restricted to short sequences and existing lncRNA prediction models narrowly focus on isolated tasks, leaving a dedicated foundation model notably absent. Here we present LncRFM, a dedicated lncRNA foundation model, supported by the LncCorpus pretraining data and the LncBench evaluation suite, which stand for a systematic framework to decode lncRNAs. For foundation model pretraining, we develop a hybrid bidirectional state-space encoder trained with a structure-guided masking strategy to effectively capture both local sequence patterns and long-range contexts. For pretraining data, we contribute over 9.6 million lncRNA sequences to assemble LncCorpus, a pretraining corpus of 24.7 million sequences. For benchmarking evaluation, we construct a comprehensive benchmark, LncBench, comprising 15 datasets and totaling over 1,010,000 sequences across 10 prediction tasks: six core lncRNA functional and annotation tasks and four structural and regulatory RNA assay tasks. Evaluated against seven RNA foundation models under a unified frozen-encoder protocol, our LncRFM achieves the state-of-the-art primary-metric scores on 11 of the 13 datasets that allow downstream adaptation. On two external generalization benchmarks evaluated without further adaptation, LncRFM matches the best structure-specialized baseline in F1 (0.141) and achieves the highest AUROC (0.962) on lncRNA contact prediction, while maintaining competitive cross-species coding-potential transfer (F1 of 0.374) under severe multi-kingdom domain shift. To benefit the scientific community, we make all datasets, source code, and pretrained models publicly available.

papers.title: rnaModScan: context-aware deep learning-based filtering of nanopore m6A and inosine calls
papers.abstract: Nanopore direct RNA sequencing (DRS) can detect multiple RNA modifications, but falsepositive background calls complicate transcriptome-wide analysis. We developed rnaModScan,a deep learning filter that integrates Dorado scores for all eight modification types with local sequence, repeat, and per-read alignment features to distinguish N6-methyladenosine (m6A) and inosine candidates from background calls. Using public RNA004 data, we evaluated site classification by grouped five-fold cross-validation and assessed transfer to HeLa cellular RNA using model weights fitted exclusively to HEK293T cellular RNA and unmodified in vitrotranscribed controls. For m6A sites outside the canonical DRACH motif, filtering removed 92.85% of the Dorado/modkit candidates while retaining 93.34% of their original matches to the GLORI reference map. The F1 score relative to DRS-covered GLORI sites increased from 3.04% to 26.76%. For inosine, filtering removed 83.44% of the candidates while preserving 99.86% of their original Slic-seq matches, and the reference-map F1 score increased from 5.22% to 22.05%. Filtering also brought the motif, repeat, and transcript-position distributions of retained candidates closer to those in the orthogonal short-read maps generated by GLORI and Slic-seq. These results support rnaModScan as a practical complement to Dorado-based RNA004 analysis for prioritizing transcriptome-wide m6A and inosine candidates.Availability: rnaModScan is available at https://github.com/uedaLabR/rnaModScan and archived in Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24546829).Keywords: direct RNA sequencing; RNA modifications; Dorado; deep learning; inosine; m6A

papers.title: GNEval: A Context-Specific Benchmark for Gene Network Inference with Single-Cell Foundation Models
papers.abstract: Gene network (GN) inference plays a critical role in understanding gene relationships and their roles in biological functions and diseases. Existing single-cell GN inference methods often rely on limited data from individual studies. Single-cell foundation models, pretrained on large and diverse datasets, provide a range of gene-gene association signals that offer a promising basis for GN inference. However, it remains unclear which GN properties these signals capture and how they compare with domain-specific methods. To address this gap, we introduce GNEval, a unified benchmark for evaluating pretrained model derived gene associations for network inference. We benchmark 21 gene representations and association scores from 11 models, including static gene embeddings (S), contextual embeddings (C), and gene-gene attention scores (A). GNEval assesses inferred networks based on their consistency with functional and perturbational evidence, including 14 Perturb-seq datasets across diverse cell systems, perturbation types and data sizes. The results reveal substantial heterogeneity across evaluation tasks and models. Rankings based on Gene Ontology and Perturb-seq evidence were nearly uncorrelated (Spearman {rho} = -0.05). Context-independent representations showed a substantial advantage in recovering functional relationships ({Delta}AUROC = 0.13), whereas context-dependent gene associations improved recovery of perturbation-associated differential expression relationships by 3.8x. The domain-specific method achieves relatively strong performance on both evidence types, offering a better balance across the two evaluations than most foundation-model-derived networks. Overall, gene representations and association scores show task-specific strengths, highlighting the need for task-aware selection and integration with domain-specific methods.

papers.title: Deep Learning-Guided Design of Candidate Synthetic Cis-Regulatory Elements for a TCF7+ Progenitor-Exhausted-like CD8+ T-Cell State
papers.abstract: Progenitor-exhausted CD8+ T cells (Tex-prog) are essential for sustaining T-cell-mediated immunity during chronic infection and cancer and therefore offer a promising immunotherapy target. Synthetic cis-regulatory elements (CREs) could enable selective transgene expression in Tex-prog cells, but whether they can distinguish this population from closely related CD8+ T-cell exhaustion states remains unclear. Here, we integrated publicly available paired single-cell ATAC-seq and single-cell RNA-seq datasets from mouse infection and tumor models and identified an ATAC-defined Tex-prog-like population (C1). We used the CREsted framework to fine-tune a pretrained Borzoi model to predict chromatin accessibility across C1 and ten comparator populations. We then used CREsted to design candidate synthetic CREs with predicted preferential accessibility in C1. The fine-tuned model achieved an average precision of 0.242 for identifying C1-selective regions on chromosomes held out from fine-tuning, approximately tenfold higher than the random-ranking baseline. Sequence optimization generated 196 1,000-bp designs with at least twofold higher predicted accessibility in C1 relative to the strongest competing population across eight DNA backgrounds. Motif enrichment and sequence-attribution analyses identified sequence patterns associated with AP-1, NFAT, POU, EGR, and TCF/LEF transcription factor families. Together, these findings identify candidate synthetic CREs with predicted preferential accessibility in a Tex-prog-like CD8+ T-cell population and provide a foundation for future experimental evaluation of their functional enhancer activity and cell-state specificity.

papers.title: MASLD-Bench evaluating language models on liver omics and fibrosis endpoints
papers.abstract: Language models may provide an interface to molecular measurements, but their ability to predict fibrosis remains uncertain. MASLD-Bench retrospectively evaluates archived model outputs from fixed liver-omics datasets. We examined 19 task datasets containing 106,688 prompts across liver transcriptomics, staged cohorts, progression, perturbation transfer and plasma cell-free RNA. Evaluated subsets comprised 15-414 items per model-task combination from 21-179 samples per family. Metrics included accuracy, mean absolute error (MAE), response-parsing coverage, 95% confidence intervals, paired differences and exact McNemar tests. The tissue analysis included 17 eligible models. On 163 common binary items, six matched majority accuracy (0.656); none exceeded it. Nemotrons five-class accuracy was 0.276 versus majority accuracy of 0.264 and uniform-choice chance of 0.200. Regression MAEs among parsed responses were 1.142 for Qwen3-1.7B v5 (162/162 parsed) and 1.517 for Llama 3.3 70B (150/162 parsed); corresponding MAEs on 150 jointly parsed items were 1.127 and 1.517. Rankings varied across formats and populations. In the second plasma cell-free RNA cohort, logistic regression achieved accuracy of 0.609 (95% CI, 0.536-0.676) with training-only per-gene preprocessing, versus majority accuracy of 0.531. With per-sample preprocessing, the interval included the majority rate. A five-gene panel selected in the reference cohort achieved external accuracy of 0.615 without established paired superiority over the majority classifier (McNemar p = 0.133). Baseline definition, training exposure, output validity and preprocessing affect interpretation. These retrospective findings establish neither clinical utility nor a general language-model advantage in fibrosis staging. Plain Language SummaryArtificial intelligence (AI) systems, including large language models, are increasingly being tested to see if they can read complex medical data and help predict disease. In this study, we evaluated several popular AI systems to see if they could predict liver scarring (fibrosis) in patients with MASLD, a common chronic liver disease. We presented the AI models with gene activity data from liver biopsies and blood samples and asked them to stage the disease. We found that none of the AI models outperformed a simple "majority rule" -- meaning no model was more accurate than simply predicting the most common outcome seen across all patients. While some models appeared to have very low error rates, this was misleading: the models were simply guessing the average patient response rather than actually learning meaningful biological patterns from the data. Our study also discovered that some models had inadvertently been trained on the very test data they were being evaluated on, which would artificially inflate their apparent performance.
