MicroDUET therefore provides a compact, reusable representation for scalable pathogen surveillance and sequence triage.

papers.title: Learning the limits of protein structure models with NMR chemical shifts
papers.abstract: Protein foundation models are intended to implicitly learn the chemical rules underlying protein function. However, systematically evaluating what biochemistry these models have learned remains difficult, as most downstream tasks lack experimental data fine-grained enough to expose their failure modes. NMR chemical shifts fill this gap: as direct per-atom reporters of local chemical environment, they offer a sensitive probe of structure-based representations. In this work, we present a systematically curated chemical shift dataset designed to minimize experimental confounders. We use it to benchmark diverse protein foundation models in their ability to predict backbone 15N chemical shifts, atoms that are known to be sensitive to many effects. The largest error across all models is in core residues with evidence of fast-timescale dynamics, which we investigate mechanistically using molecular dynamics simulations. Given the biological relevance of structured dynamic regions, we trained a new model based on the best of these embeddings, SLAE, to predict its own error. SLAE-ERR achieves a mean absolute error of 0.76 ppm for predicting error. Together, we hope that the datasets, evaluation tasks, and models presented here are sources of guidance for protein design model improvement.

papers.title: Deep learning-guided discovery reveals the diversity and mutational potential of environmental beta-lactamases
papers.abstract: Beta-lactamases are a major mechanism of bacterial resistance to beta-lactam antibiotics; however, their functional diversity and mutational potential in environmental microbial communities remain partially understood. This study aimed to characterize environmental beta-lactamase diversity and investigate how sequence variation influences antibiotic resistance. By integrating protein language model (PLMs) with ensemble learning, we identified more than 46,000 putative beta-lactamases across all four Ambler classes from environmental metagenomes, widely distributed across diverse habitats, with distinct habitat-associated class compositions. The candidates sharing approximately 30% sequence identity with known beta-lactamases conferred resistance to multiple beta-lactam antibiotics when expressed in Escherichia coli. Combining inverse folding model with PLMs further identified mutations that altered resistance profiles, including substitutions that increased resistance to carbapenems. Predicted high-fitness sites exhibited greater natural sequence variability overall, with higher variability in wastewater-derived than ocean-derived enzymes. These findings reveal undercharacterized beta-lactamase diversity and substantial mutational flexibility in environmental microbiomes, providing a basis for investigating their potential contribution to the diversification of antibiotic resistance.

papers.title: DBAASP V4: condition-resolved bioactivity and chemical structures for data-driven peptide and peptidomimetic discovery.
papers.abstract: The current peptide renaissance-driven by metagenomic and proteomic mining, molecular de-extinction, protein language models, and generative or evolutionary design-is producing millions of candidates, but useful machine learning depends on experimentally anchored, context-rich labels. The Database of Antimicrobial Activity and Structure of Peptides (DBAASP) is a manually curated resource linking peptides and peptidomimetics to quantitative antimicrobial, antibiofilm, anticancer, hemolytic, and mammalian-cell cytotoxicity measurements and their experimental conditions. DBAASP v4 contains >25 000 entries and extends the resource from a sequence-centered database to a structure-aware repository. Major additions include systematic SMILES representations, enhanced annotation of intrachain bonds and ring architectures, dedicated antibiofilm, and synergy records, PubChem links, >9200 molecular-dynamics trajectories, and new prediction services. The condition-resolved data support supervised learning, strain-, and target-specific models, model calibration, and surrogate fitness functions for genetic algorithms. SMILES representations further enable modeling of noncanonical peptides and peptidomimetics that cannot be adequately described by sequence alone. DBAASP therefore complements large peptide catalogues by providing the experimentally curated activity and structure layers, needed to convert sequence information into testable predictions, design, and optimization of biologically active compounds. DBAASP v4 is freely available at https://dbaasp.org.

papers.title: Biobank-scale self-supervised genotype pretraining yields transferable representations for human genetics.
papers.abstract: Biobank-scale genotyping has created unprecedented cohorts for human genetics, yet the field still lacks scalable methods for learning transferable representations from largely unlabeled individual-level genotype data. Here, we introduce SNPBERT, a self-supervised transformer pretrained on genotypes from 485 923 UK Biobank participants using masked rsID prediction. SNPBERT embeddings recovered known population structure across UK Biobank and three external datasets, performed comparably to principal component analysis, and supported the identification of ancestry-informative marker SNPs. Fine-tuning with an attention-based multiple-instance head generated disease-specific risk scores that provided complementary information beyond conventional polygenic risk scores. The relative increase in Nagelkerke's R2 ranged from 0.7% to 3.3%, and independent associations were observed for seven of the eight chronic diseases examined. In celiac disease, attention prioritization recapitulated major histocompatibility complex signals while elevating variants in CCHCR1 and NOTCH4 relative to genome-wide association study (GWAS) ranking. These results support biobank-scale genotype pretraining as an early step toward foundation modeling for individual-level genotype data.

papers.title: A Three-Axis Framework for Therapy Prioritization in MBD4-Deficient Tumors: De-confounded Synthetic Lethality Modeling, Replication-Stress Pharmacology, and PARP1 Trapping Decoupling
papers.abstract: Background: Loss-of-function mutations in MBD4 (methyl-CpG-binding domain protein 4) cause a specialized base excision repair (BER) deficiency characterized by hypermutated CpG>TpG signatures and sensitivity to immune checkpoint blockade. However, post-immunotherapy treatment prioritization remains empirically unmapped. In clinical oncology, DNA damage response (DDR) defects are frequently extrapolated to poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibitor (PARPi) sensitivity by analogy to homologous recombination deficiency (HRD), without testing whether upstream glycosylase loss generates the nicked single-strand break (SSB) intermediates required for toxic PARP1-DNA trapping. Methods: We developed a three-axis framework integrating mechanistic curation, large-scale pharmacogenomics (DepMap 24Q2 CRISPR/RNA-seq, n=1,517; GDSC2 dose-response profiling, n=928; PRISM Repurposing), and a 5-Layer De-confounded Synthetic Lethality Machine Learning (SL-ML) Engine (SL-XGBRanker). To prevent functional dilution from variants of uncertain significance, MBD4 loss-of-function (MBD4-LOF) was strictly restricted to truncating and canonical splice-site alleles (21 of 36 mutated lines), independently validated by nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD; two-sided p2s = 0.0367), while excluding 15 lines harboring 19 non-truncating variants (18 missense, 1 inframe deletion). All primary pharmacogenomic comparisons were evaluated using two-sided Mann-Whitney U tests (p2s), bootstrap 95% confidence intervals (CIs), Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (BH-FDR) multiplicity correction across six pre-specified candidate axes, and Two One-Sided Tests (TOST) for expression equivalence. Results: Our analysis delineates three distinct therapeutic axes in MBD4-LOF tumors: (1) Cytidine Analog Vulnerability (Axis 1): Mechanistic structural evidence demonstrates that MBD4 loss impairs excision of 5-substituted pyrimidine analogs and deaminated bases, creating a direct biochemical bottleneck to gemcitabine and 5-fluorouracil incorporation. (2) ATR-Check1 Replication-Stress Vulnerability (Axis 2): In GDSC2 profiling, MBD4-LOF cell lines exhibit significant sensitivity to the ATR inhibitor ceralasertib (AZD6738). In the clinically relevant TP53-mutant background-which disables the G1/S checkpoint and forces reliance on ATR-mediated S/G2 arrest-MBD4-LOF lines (n=11 vs n=619 WT) demonstrate pronounced ceralasertib hypersensitivity (Delta LN_IC50 = -1.07, 95% CI [-1.62, -0.41], Cohen's d = -0.74, p2s = 0.0060, BH-FDR q = 0.036; Delta AUC = -0.087, d = -0.89, p2s = 0.0017), with 11/11 leave-one-out (LOO) jackknife iterations retaining two-sided significance (p2s <= 0.014). This genotype-associated dependency remains robust in the unstratified pan-cancer cohort (n=14 vs n=914 WT; Delta LN_IC50 = -0.73, 95% CI [-1.31, -0.11], d = -0.50, p2s = 0.0430; Delta AUC = -0.056, d = -0.56, p2s = 0.0259) and after purging microsatellite instability-high (MSI-H) lines (n=10 vs n=906 WT MSS; Delta LN_IC50 = -0.9

papers.title: Epiformer: epistasis detection by genome language model and dual-channel network.
papers.abstract: Epistasis plays a crucial role in explaining missing heritability in complex traits, yet most detection methods fail to effectively capture local and global interaction patterns and long-range dependencies critical to complex trait architecture. We propose Epiformer that leverages genome language model Evo 2 to capture long-range dependencies from genetic background, and a dual-channel network to jointly model local and global epistasis and additive effects. Epiformer can identify key SNPs and their interactions from complex genomic data to empower phenotype prediction with interpretability, which reinforces epistasis detection. Epiformer performs robustly across species, revealing biologically meaningful patterns and offering new insights into genetic architecture.

papers.title: Integer quantized multilayer perceptron neural network for lossless compression of nanopore signal.
papers.abstract: Nanopore sequencing is indispensable for advanced genomic analyses, but the raw signal output creates substantial storage and bandwidth demands. Specialized model-free compressors such as VBZ and ex-zd have been proposed to address this challenge. They deliver high throughput and strong compression performance, yet they cannot fully exploit higher-order statistical dependencies, which limits further gains. Learning-based compressors can achieve better compression ratios, but they often introduce floating-point non-determinism and are too slow for large-scale nanopore datasets, reducing their practicality. We introduce SigComp, a learned lossless compressor for nanopore signal data. SigComp employs a compact multilayer perceptron network with a fixed context window to capture higher-order dependencies within the dominant one-byte signal deltas. By integrating post-training quantization and a fully GPU-native range coder, SigComp eliminates GPU-CPU synchronization overhead in the autoregressive coding loop while ensuring strict bit-exactness across diverse execution settings. Evaluations on diverse species and sequencing chemistries (DNA R10.4.1 and RNA004) demonstrate that SigComp consistently reduces compressed file sizes by 6.00%-7.09% and 3.86%-5.34% over VBZ and ex-zd, respectively, albeit with a 10× lower processing throughput. Compared to the leading neural compressor, SigComp achieves a comparable compression ratio, sacrificing merely 0.4%-1.9%, while delivering 46-74× higher throughput. Ablation studies confirm that SigComp's integer-only, GPU-native approach improves throughput by 7.75-8.30× overall over hybrid GPU-CPU pipelines without model quantization, and the default 64-symbol context window effectively captures the vast majority of exploitable redundancy. SigComp can also be extended to lossy compression by eliminating the least significant bits, and achieve compression ratios of 4.047-4.868, outperforming lossy ex-zd by 9.18%-14.38%. Although processing remains slower than specialized codecs, SigComp offers an excellent trade-off for long-term cold archival storage, particularly when scaled via multi-GPU environments. SigComp is freely available on GitHub at: https://github.com/BioinfoSZU/SigComp. It supports CPU-only, NVIDIA, and AMD GPU execution backends with seamless cross-platform archive interoperability, as well as multi-GPU scaling. Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.

papers.title: DeepHel: improving the accuracy and completeness of Helitron annotation with a multistage deep learning framework.
papers.abstract: Accurate and comprehensive annotation of Helitrons remains challenging due to weak structural signals, ambiguous termini, sequence fragmentation, and complex nested insertions. Existing methods often exhibit limited sensitivity, high false-positive rates, and insufficient support for simultaneous detection of both HLE1 and HLE2, leading to incomplete and imprecise annotation. We present DeepHel, a multistage deep learning framework that improves the accuracy and completeness of Helitron annotation by modeling intactness, boundary characteristics, and structural consistency. DeepHel formulates Helitron detection as a staged representation learning problem, integrating sequence features, structural signals, and multiple sequence alignment information across four coordinated modules: candidate identification, intact element recognition, boundary refinement, and Helitron classification, followed by nested insertion removal. Benchmarking across five eukaryotic genomes under three evaluation settings demonstrates that DeepHel achieves a superior balance between sensitivity and precision compared with existing tools, including HiTE, HELIANO, HelitronScanner, RepeatModeler2, and EDTA. In particular, DeepHel improves the recovery of intact Helitron families (completeness), while maintaining robust performance in challenging scenarios such as low-copy elements and genomes with complex nested insertions. Furthermore, DeepHel identifies previously unannotated Helitrons with well-defined structural features, providing additional insights into Helitron diversity and genome organization. These results show that DeepHel provides a robust and comprehensive solution for accurate and complete annotation of both HLE1 and HLE2 across diverse eukaryotic genomes. DeepHel is freely available at GitHub: https://github.com/lyysxb/DeepHel, with the archived version at Zenodo: https://zenodo.org/records/22069775.

papers.title: AI-based precision prognostics and therapy personalization for childhood brain tumors.
papers.abstract: Accurate prediction of patient outcomes remains a critical challenge in oncology, in particular for childhood brain tumors, in which treatment decisions need to carefully balance risk of tumor recurrence and death against severe therapy-induced sequelae. Here, we developed MANTIS (methylation profiling and artificial neural networks for time-dependent individualized survival predictions), a precision artificial intelligence (AI) tool for medulloblastoma and ependymoma outcome prediction built on genome-wide DNA methylation array data from 2,786 patients. MANTIS generates individualized survival probabilities over a 10-year period and achieves concordance indices as high as 0.80 ± 0.07, significantly exceeding the predictive accuracy of current clinical indicators. Extending MANTIS to estimate individualized treatment effects identifies ~60% of patients with average-risk medulloblastoma without a significant survival disadvantage (P = 0.683) when treated with less intensive craniospinal irradiation doses, which is associated with improved neurocognitive outcomes. In conclusion, our study establishes a foundation for AI-based precision prognostics and therapy personalization in childhood brain tumors and offers a blueprint for similar initiatives in other cancer types.

papers.title: Narrative-based explainable artificial intelligence for precision oncology survival prediction.
papers.abstract: Explainable and accurate survival prediction (SP) remains an open challenge in Precision Oncology. Early SP methods achieved interpretability through simple models, often at the expense of prediction performance. More recent machine learning (ML) methods can learn complex patterns, but they often resemble inscrutable black boxes. Here, we propose SurvXAI, a new framework that combines reliable SP with the latest eXplainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) approach. We first train a Random Survival Forest model to predict the survival function of each patient. We then interpret these predictions by extracting patient-specific feature contributions with SurvSHAP, and we feed them into locally deployed Large Language Models (LLMs) to translate the numeric individual-level interpretation of the SP into natural language narrative explanations. Since conventional numerical breakdowns of the features' contributions to the final predictions are often perceived as unintuitive to non-ML experts, SurvXAI overcomes this limitation by automatically translating them into narrative explanations that can be readily used by clinicians to facilitate the interpretation of model predictions. We validated our SP pipeline on six oncological datasets, including an in-house Multiple Myeloma cohort, comparing it with nine state-of-the-art SP predictors. We then quantified the quality and usefulness of SurvXAI narrative explanations with a blind evaluation carried out by seven human experts. This evaluation showed that larger LLMs produced more coherent explanations with accurate feature ranking and clinically plausible reasoning. SurvXAI demonstrates the potential of integrating explainable SP with LLMs to enable trustworthy, personalized interpretation in oncology and other clinical fields. SurvXAI is available at https://github.com/AI-for-Genome-Interpretation-lab/SurvXAI_pipeline. The module for narrative generation is available at https://github.com/AI-for-Genome-Interpretation-lab/SurvXAI_stories.

papers.title: Protein resource allocation across subcellular compartments revealed by large-scale absolute quantitative proteomics in yeast.
papers.abstract: Subcellular compartmentalization within complex membrane-bound organelles is a hallmark of eukaryal life, enabling metabolic specialization through spatial segregation. Here, we compiled a dataset encompassing 300 absolute quantitative proteomes, the largest to date, across two yeast species under diverse experimental conditions. Leveraging big data analysis, formula fitting, and machine learning, quantitative correlations among protein abundance, resource allocation, and cellular phenotypes were elucidated at a system level. We found that subcellular resource distribution is highly uneven and covaries with specific growth rate. Specifically, at high specific growth rates, the protein mass fraction (PMF) from certain compartments, (e.g., nucleus) is consistently reduced, coinciding with the increasing protein resource demand from ribosomes. Meanwhile, nutrient limitation may induce resource recycling by upregulating protein resources within specific compartments (e.g., vacuole) to sustain stress adaptation. Importantly, our integrative analysis indicates that PMF from a few subcellular compartments (e.g., nucleus and ribosomes) can accurately predict yeast physiological parameters (e.g., specific growth rate, oxygen uptake rate), and a limited protein set (≥ 23) could be used to capture the variation in resource allocation across seven major subcellular compartments. Furthermore, our comparative analysis between Crabtree-positive and Crabtree-negative species across conditions illustrates that subcellular resource allocation could be shaped by multiple factors and the two species differ markedly in their robustness to environmental perturbations. In summary, the high-quality quantitative proteomic dataset for yeast species offers an unprecedented opportunity for understanding the general principles underlying subcellular resource allocation, laying foundations for precision engineering of cell factories in synthetic biology.
papers.venue: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A

papers.title: YAP1-induced super-enhancer rewiring mediates gene-environment-driven malignant reprogramming and metastatic ecosystem formation in head and neck cancer
papers.abstract: Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) is characterized by frequent TP53 mutations, which are insufficient for tumorigenesis and largely undruggable, underscoring the need to define epigenetic mechanisms driving cancer evolution. Here we show that TP53 mutation facilitates YAP1-dependent transcriptional reprogramming, driving epigenetic tumor evolution by hijacking tissue-regenerative programs. Integrated multi-omics analyses of mouse models and multiregional human HNSCC samples reveal that global chromatin architecture remains largely stable during progression, whereas YAP1 dynamically redistributes to newly formed super-enhancers accompanied by enhancer DNA hypomethylation. Mechanistically, YAP1 establishes an IL6-dependent feedforward loop and cooperates with stage-specific transcription factors, including FOXM1, DeltaNp63, and PITX2. The YAP1-PITX2 axis promotes partial EMT, cancer-associated fibroblast activation, and lymph node metastasis, resulting in a fibrotic and immunosuppressive metastatic ecosystem. These findings identify a YAP1-driven epigenetic circuit as a central hub linking environmental stress to malignant reprogramming and highlight a potential therapeutic vulnerability in HNSCC.

papers.title: Single-cell study of the FCG rat model and cross-species comparison reveal stronger gene regulation by sex chromosome complement in the medial septum
papers.abstract: Sex differences are prominent in neuropsychiatric, neurological, and neurodegenerative conditions. While both gonads (ovaries vs. testes) and sex chromosome complement (SCC; XX vs. XY) contribute to sex differences, these effects are hard to differentiate in humans and gonadal contributions have been considered dominant in the brain. The four core genotypes (FCG) mouse model distinguishes between SCC and gonadal effects but whether findings are conserved across species remains unclear. Here, we present the first application of the novel FCG-derived rat model to explore cell-type-specific sex differences in the medial septum (MS), which shows robust structural sex differences, and convergence/divergence between species. Differential gene expression, pathway, transcription factor, and gene regulatory network analyses show dominant SCC effects and concordant gonadal effects on gene and network regulation in rat MS cell types. Comparison between the FCG rat and mouse models find convergence across species on the dominance of the SCC in regulating gene expression in concert with gonadal effects in the MS, despite divergence in individual sex-biased genes. In both species, the sex-biased, cell-type-specific MS genes and networks are associated with diverse diseases relevant to MS functions, such as anxiety, Alzheimers Disease, epilepsy, and schizophrenia, that can be targeted by proposed therapeutic candidates. Our cross-species investigation identifies a conserved dominance of SCC effects in sex-biased gene expression in the MS, thereby challenging the classical gonad-centric view of sexual differentiation in the brain and highlighting the MS as an important region for the study of sex differences driven by the sex chromosome complement.

papers.title: Deep Learning Prediction of DNA Damage Response Protein Signaling from H&E Histopathology and Reverse-Phase Protein Arrays in Pan-Gynecologic and Breast Cancers
papers.abstract: Defects in homologous recombination and the DNA damage response (DDR) make gynecologic and breast tumors sensitive to platinum chemotherapy and PARP inhibitors, but identifying them requires costly genomic testing that reads permanent genomic scars rather than current pathway activity. Routine hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) slides are available for nearly every patient. This project asked whether H&E morphology carries information about functional DDR protein signaling across five cancer types in a single model. We matched 1,673 diagnostic whole-slide images from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) to Level 4 reverse-phase protein array (RPPA) data for 1,527 patients with breast (BRCA, n = 858), endometrial (UCEC, n = 403), cervical (CESC, n = 146), ovarian (OV, n = 72), and uterine carcinosarcoma (UCS, n = 48) tumors. Slides were tiled at 0.5 m/px and Macenko-normalized, yielding 20.4 million tiles. Tiles were embedded with two frozen pathology foundation models, UNI2-h and Virchow2. A gated attention-based multiple instance learning (ABMIL) network jointly regressed six RPPA pathway scores, including a DNA_damage composite of 11 DDR proteins. Performance was assessed by out-of-fold Spearman correlation under 5-fold, cancer-type-stratified, site-grouped cross-validation and compared against a baseline that predicts each patient's cancer-type mean. Predicted DNA_damage correlated with measured values ({rho} = 0.43 for both encoders) and exceeded the cancer-type baseline ({rho} = 0.31; {Delta} {rho} = +0.13). The signal held within cancer types (within-type {rho} = 0.29 for UNI2-h, 0.30 for Virchow2). With the original UNI encoder, it survived site-held-out folds with residualized targets (within-type {rho} = 0.26), and it vanished when targets were shuffled within cancer type (within-type {rho} [≤] 0.00 for all three encoders). All six pathway scores were predicted above baseline; Cell_cycle was strongest ({rho} {approx} 0.59). In interpretability analyses, the top 10 attention tiles per slide contained more tumor (+1.8 SD), larger tumor nuclei (+1.0 to +1.3 SD), and fewer lymphocytes (-0.6 SD) than the bottom 10 tiles; 13 of 14 morphometric features differed (q < 0.05). Attention agreed with Integrated Gradients (median {rho} {approx} 0.70). Routine H&E contains a moderate, reproducible signal of DDR protein abundance beyond cancer type, concentrated in tumor-dense regions with enlarged nuclei. Separating this signal from proliferation and predicting phosphorylated CHK1 and CHK2 directly are the next steps toward a functional, slide-based DDR biomarker.

papers.title: Scalable and Synthesizable DNA Library Design via Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Designing DNA libraries is a key challenge from drug design to protein engineering and synthetic biology. Modern generative models offer opportunities to navigate the design space and propose specific sequences predicted to be effective in-silico. Designing deterministic libraries of specific sequences is however limited by the cost of DNA synthesis -- the synthesis barrier. In contrast, high-throughput multiplexed screening can measure the function of billions of biological sequences in parallel. Harnessing this technology requires the design of randomized libraries with specific design constraints to achieve low synthesis costs. In practice, such stochastic libraries are often chosen heuristically, sacrificing control for scale. Is there a way to bridge AI-based in-silico sequence design with high-throughput experimentation? In this work, we introduce Policy Gradients for Library Design (PGLD). PGLD uses a synthesis-aware parameterization of stochastic DNA libraries and optimizes them against a specified objective function. This allows for designing massive, controlled libraries without being limited by synthesis costs. We show how PGLD enables lab-in-the-loop design of multi-round high-throughput experiments, and large-scale in-vitro DNA sampling from generative models. Finally, we use PGLD to design a library of ~10^6 unique sequences at a cost of ~700 USD to explore the mutation space of a broadly neutralizing influenza antibody.

papers.title: Substrate rigidity suppresses the NRF2 antioxidant program in breast cancer cells
papers.abstract: Matrix stiffness rises as breast tumors progress, but whether rigidity raises or lowers activity of the KEAP1-NRF2 antioxidant pathway is contested: work in breast cancer cells places the antioxidant response on soft matrix, while work in liver cancer places response on stiff. We used publicly available transcriptome data to ask the question across laboratories rather than within one system. Of eleven series identified, four dataset arms passed quality criteria fixed before any biological analysis. Across five contrasts spanning three cell lines and two matrix formats, one program responded in the same direction every time: the NRF2 antioxidant battery was lower on the more rigid substrate in all five. In contrast, SLC7A11, the cystine transporter supporting glutathione synthesis, decreased in all five, by up to 6.5-fold. YAP and TEAD targets did not track rigidity, rising on hydrogels and glass but falling on cell-derived matrix. NFE2L2 and its regulators were unchanged, while targets fell in proportion to their dependence on the antioxidant response element, pointing to control after transcription. An unsupervised partition made without reference to any pathway recovered the same program and survived removal of proliferation genes. In 1,097 TCGA and 1,980 METABRIC breast tumors, the matrix proxy was unrelated to the full battery until immune and hypoxic composition were accounted for, after which the same negative direction appeared in both; and a tumor-intrinsic score excluding macrophage-expressed members showed it more directly. Single-cell and spatial tests produced the predicted direction but could not resolve it, due to limited sample size and because the genes carrying the effect are largely undetectable at spot depth. Reduced antioxidant capacity on rigid substrate predicts greater sensitivity to agents killing through lipid peroxidation, a prediction we set out for experimental test.

papers.title: ADSMoE: A mixture-of-experts-based transformer autoencoder for discovering multimodal Alzheimer's disease subtypes
papers.abstract: Alzheimers disease (AD) exhibits substantial biological and clinical heterogeneity, posing critical challenges for advancing precision medicine. Existing data-driven approaches often rely on modality-specific clustering or predefined biomarker trajectories, limiting their ability to discover disease subtypes from incomplete, heterogeneous real-world data. In this study, we introduce ADSMoE, a mixture-of-experts (MoE)-based multimodal representation learning framework that jointly identifies AD subtypes as latent disease signatures while accommodating incomplete modality combinations. ADSMoE integrates a Fleximodal MoE encoder that accommodates arbitrary combinations of available modalities with a novel subtype-specific MoE decoder to capture complementary disease characteristics through expert specialization. Using data from 5,422 participants across three independent cohorts, we trained ADSMoE on the ADNI cohort and externally validated the identified subtypes in NACC and UKB without model retraining. The proposed ADSMoE identified four AD subtypes with distinct neuroimaging patterns, genetic and proteomic associations, and clinical characteristics. Benchmarking analyses demonstrated robust subtype discovery and strong biological and clinical relevance, while external validation revealed consistent subtype-associated characteristics across independent cohorts. ADSMoE advances AD subtyping by uncovering biologically and clinically meaningful AD heterogeneity from incomplete multimodal data, providing a scalable framework for disease stratification, biomarker discovery, and future precision medicine applications in AD.

papers.title: DeepTTA: a transformer-based model for predicting cancer drug response
papers.abstract: Identifying new lead molecules to treat cancer requires more than a decade of dedicated effort. Before selected drug candidates are used in the clinic, their anti-cancer activity is generally validated by in vitro cellular experiments. Therefore, accurate prediction of cancer drug response is a critical and challenging task for anti-cancer drugs design and precision medicine. With the development of pharmacogenomics, the combination of efficient drug feature extraction methods and omics data has made it possible to use computational models to assist in drug response prediction. In this study, we propose DeepTTA, a novel end-to-end deep learning model that utilizes transformer for drug representation learning and a multilayer neural network for transcriptomic data prediction of the anti-cancer drug responses. Specifically, DeepTTA uses transcriptomic gene expression data and chemical substructures of drugs for drug response prediction. Compared to existing methods, DeepTTA achieved higher performance in terms of root mean square error, Pearson correlation coefficient and Spearman's rank correlation coefficient on multiple test sets. Moreover, we discovered that anti-cancer drugs bortezomib and dactinomycin provide a potential therapeutic option with multiple clinical indications. With its excellent performance, DeepTTA is expected to be an effective method in cancer drug design.

papers.title: Single-cell spatial landscapes of the lung tumour immune microenvironment
papers.abstract: Abstract Single-cell technologies have revealed the complexity of the tumour immune microenvironment with unparalleled resolution 1–9 . Most clinical strategies rely on histopathological stratification of tumour subtypes, yet the spatial context of single-cell phenotypes within these stratified subgroups is poorly understood. Here we apply imaging mass cytometry to characterize the tumour and immunological landscape of samples from 416 patients with lung adenocarcinoma across five histological patterns. We resolve more than 1.6 million cells, enabling spatial analysis of immune lineages and activation states with distinct clinical correlates, including survival. Using deep learning, we can predict with high accuracy those patients who will progress after surgery using a single 1-mm 2 tumour core, which could be informative for clinical management following surgical resection. Our dataset represents a valuable resource for the non-small cell lung cancer research community and exemplifies the utility of spatial resolution within single-cell analyses. This study also highlights how artificial intelligence can improve our understanding of microenvironmental features that underlie cancer progression and may influence future clinical practice.

papers.title: Integrating Unsupervised Clustering with Transformer-Based Models for De Novo Cell Population Identification
papers.abstract: Single-cell transcriptome sequencing has been widely applied across the life sciences. It enables accurate and robust identification of cell types in heterogeneous biological tissues through unsupervised clustering, shallow learning, and deep learning. While deep learning does not outperform shallow learning in classification performance, it streamlines cell type identification by eliminating cumbersome preprocessing procedures. However, the availability of training datasets with comprehensive cell type annotations is always limited, so new datasets inevitably contain cell populations that are not pre-defined in the training data. To address this limitation, we integrated unsupervised clustering with transformer-based models to identify cell populations unrecognized by classical methods. Specifically, we developed the Nankai GeneRank Classifier by fine-tuning the pre-trained Geneformer-V1 model, and then clustered cells based on its softmax-normalized class probability matrix (SCPM). Applied to a public colorectal cancer dataset, the new method, named SCPM-based clustering, resolved cell populations that cannot be unambiguously identified by classical methods alone and led to the discovery of novel candidate markers of colorectal cancer stem cells, demonstrating its utility.

papers.title: Revolutionizing Pharmaceutical Research: Harnessing Machine Learning for a Paradigm Shift in Drug Discovery
papers.abstract: The fusion of machine learning (ML) and artificial intelligence (AI) is experiencing a dramatic transition in the field of pharmaceutical research and development. This study examines the several effects of machine learning (ML) on different phases of medication discovery, development, and patient care. The capability of ML to quickly process huge chemical libraries and forecast interactions with target proteins is studied, starting with compound screening and selection. The potential for fewer false positives and negatives, improved hit prediction accuracy, and ensemble technique use are underlined. The part that machine learning plays in enhancing Absorption, Distribution, Metabolism, Excretion, and Toxicity (ADMET) profile is then explained. ML models anticipate compound actions inside the human body by analyzing molecular structures and characteristics, improving assessments of drug safety and efficacy. The article goes into further detail about predictive modeling, highlighting how machine learning may be used to find prospective therapeutic targets and confirm their applicability. The combination of multi-omics data, deep learning, and the possibility to identify similar molecular pathways across diseases highlight the game-changing potential of machine learning in this field. The article also covers the use of ML in clinical trials, highlighting its benefits for trial planning, patient recruitment, real-time monitoring, and individualized therapy predictions. By utilizing computational analysis and quantum physics, the power of machine learning-driven de novo drug creation is examined, revealing the potential to develop new therapeutic candidates. In this article, the ethical issues surrounding AI-driven drug discovery are discussed, with a focus on the necessity of transparent data utilization, human oversight, and responsible data consumption. The report ends by predicting ML's potential for pharmaceutical R&D in the future. Accelerated drug discovery pipelines, the rise of customized medicine powered by predictive models, optimized clinical trials, and a change in medication repurposing tactics are all envisaged in this. The report emphasizes the revolutionary potential of ML in altering pharmaceutical research and development while noting obstacles in data quality, model interpretability, ethics, and interdisciplinary collaboration. It is suggested that the ethical integration of AI technologies, interdisciplinary cooperation, and regulatory modifications are essential steps to unlock the full potential of ML and AI and, ultimately, provide patients throughout the world with safer, more efficient, and individualized treatments.
papers.venue: International Journal of Multidisciplinary Sciences and Arts

papers.title: DynamicBind: predicting ligand-specific protein-ligand complex structure with a deep equivariant generative model
papers.abstract: While significant advances have been made in predicting static protein structures, the inherent dynamics of proteins, modulated by ligands, are crucial for understanding protein function and facilitating drug discovery. Traditional docking methods, frequently used in studying protein-ligand interactions, typically treat proteins as rigid. While molecular dynamics simulations can propose appropriate protein conformations, they're computationally demanding due to rare transitions between biologically relevant equilibrium states. In this study, we present DynamicBind, a deep learning method that employs equivariant geometric diffusion networks to construct a smooth energy landscape, promoting efficient transitions between different equilibrium states. DynamicBind accurately recovers ligand-specific conformations from unbound protein structures without the need for holo-structures or extensive sampling. Remarkably, it demonstrates state-of-the-art performance in docking and virtual screening benchmarks. Our experiments reveal that DynamicBind can accommodate a wide range of large protein conformational changes and identify cryptic pockets in unseen protein targets. As a result, DynamicBind shows potential in accelerating the development of small molecules for previously undruggable targets and expanding the horizons of computational drug discovery.

papers.title: DeepImpute: an accurate, fast, and scalable deep neural network method to impute single-cell RNA-seq data
papers.abstract: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) offers new opportunities to study gene expression of tens of thousands of single cells simultaneously. We present DeepImpute, a deep neural network-based imputation algorithm that uses dropout layers and loss functions to learn patterns in the data, allowing for accurate imputation. Overall, DeepImpute yields better accuracy than other six publicly available scRNA-seq imputation methods on experimental data, as measured by the mean squared error or Pearson's correlation coefficient. DeepImpute is an accurate, fast, and scalable imputation tool that is suited to handle the ever-increasing volume of scRNA-seq data, and is freely available at https://github.com/lanagarmire/DeepImpute .

papers.title: DNNGP, a deep neural network-based method for genomic prediction using multi-omics data in plants
papers.abstract: Genomic prediction is an effective way to accelerate the rate of agronomic trait improvement in plants. Traditional methods typically use linear regression models with clear assumptions; such methods are unable to capture the complex relationships between genotypes and phenotypes. Non-linear models (e.g., deep neural networks) have been proposed as a superior alternative to linear models because they can capture complex non-additive effects. Here we introduce a deep learning (DL) method, deep neural network genomic prediction (DNNGP), for integration of multi-omics data in plants. We trained DNNGP on four datasets and compared its performance with methods built with five classic models: genomic best linear unbiased prediction (GBLUP); two methods based on a machine learning (ML) framework, light gradient boosting machine (LightGBM) and support vector regression (SVR); and two methods based on a DL framework, deep learning genomic selection (DeepGS) and deep learning genome-wide association study (DLGWAS). DNNGP is novel in five ways. First, it can be applied to a variety of omics data to predict phenotypes. Second, the multilayered hierarchical structure of DNNGP dynamically learns features from raw data, avoiding overfitting and improving the convergence rate using a batch normalization layer and early stopping and rectified linear activation (rectified linear unit) functions. Third, when small datasets were used, DNNGP produced results that are competitive with results from the other five methods, showing greater prediction accuracy than the other methods when large-scale breeding data were used. Fourth, the computation time required by DNNGP was comparable with that of commonly used methods, up to 10 times faster than DeepGS. Fifth, hyperparameters can easily be batch tuned on a local machine. Compared with GBLUP, LightGBM, SVR, DeepGS and DLGWAS, DNNGP is superior to these existing widely used genomic selection (GS) methods. Moreover, DNNGP can generate robust assessments from diverse datasets, including omics data, and quickly incorporate complex and large datasets into usable models, making it a promising and practical approach for straightforward integration into existing GS platforms.

papers.title: Deep Learning–Based Multi-Omics Integration Robustly Predicts Survival in Liver Cancer
papers.abstract: Identifying robust survival subgroups of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) will significantly improve patient care. Currently, endeavor of integrating multi-omics data to explicitly predict HCC survival from multiple patient cohorts is lacking. To fill this gap, we present a deep learning (DL)–based model on HCC that robustly differentiates survival subpopulations of patients in six cohorts. We built the DL-based, survival-sensitive model on 360 HCC patients' data using RNA sequencing (RNA-Seq), miRNA sequencing (miRNA-Seq), and methylation data from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA), which predicts prognosis as good as an alternative model where genomics and clinical data are both considered. This DL-based model provides two optimal subgroups of patients with significant survival differences (P = 7.13e−6) and good model fitness [concordance index (C-index) = 0.68]. More aggressive subtype is associated with frequent TP53 inactivation mutations, higher expression of stemness markers (KRT19 and EPCAM) and tumor marker BIRC5, and activated Wnt and Akt signaling pathways. We validated this multi-omics model on five external datasets of various omics types: LIRI-JP cohort (n = 230, C-index = 0.75), NCI cohort (n = 221, C-index = 0.67), Chinese cohort (n = 166, C-index = 0.69), E-TABM-36 cohort (n = 40, C-index = 0.77), and Hawaiian cohort (n = 27, C-index = 0.82). This is the first study to employ DL to identify multi-omics features linked to the differential survival of patients with HCC. Given its robustness over multiple cohorts, we expect this workflow to be useful at predicting HCC prognosis prediction. Clin Cancer Res; 24(6); 1248–59. ©2017 AACR.

papers.title: GTRD 2026: expanded content and resources for deep learning.
papers.abstract: Gene Transcription Regulation Database (GTRD; https://gtrd.biouml.org/) contains uniformly annotated and processed NGS data related to transcription regulation: ChIP-seq, ChIP-exo, DNase-seq, MNase-seq, ATAC-seq, and RNA-seq. The latest release significantly extends the number of available experiments. All new ChIP-seq data for human transcription factors (TFs) obtained by the Codebook Consortium were processed and annotated; GTRD now covers 85% of all known human TFs. We added new types of information related to transcription regulation: enhancer regions revealed from analysis of CAGE-seq data and single-cell ATAC-seq data. To facilitate the use of GTRD for building deep learning models, we provide direct access to the MySQL database where metadata are stored and have built profiles with single-nucleotide resolution for ChIP-seq and ATAC-seq data.

papers.title: A defence-in-depth strategy for securing AI-driven biological sequence design.
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence can design biological sequences, from proteins to whole genomes, opening opportunities for medicine and biotechnology, but the same capability can be misused. The Wübben Sandpit conference brought together experts in biology, AI, biosecurity, ethics, medicine and policy to ask how the field can capture the benefits while managing the risks. Here we set out a defence-in-depth strategy that builds safeguards into every stage, from the data used to train models, to the models themselves, to the synthesis of physical DNA. We argue that responsible governance is not a brake on progress but a precondition for it.

papers.title: Large-scale proteomic characterization reveals clinically relevant subtypes of early-stage papillary thyroid cancer for prognostic prediction.
papers.abstract: Papillary thyroid cancer (PTC) has a rising incidence. The majority are diagnosed at an early stage, albeit with a minority exhibiting aggressive tendencies. Given its generally indolent nature, controversy persists regarding the management of early-stage PTCs, particularly surgical intervention and long-term surveillance strategies. Here, we conduct a large-scale proteomic characterization of early-stage PTC based on tumor samples from 797 patients. Proteomic profiling unveils clinically relevant modules and identifies six subtypes, capturing the spectrum of heterogeneity from indolent to progressive disease states. Notably, subtypes associated with higher progression risk display enhanced signatures of ribogenesis and epithelial-mesenchymal transition. Furthermore, integrating machine learning with protein co-expression network analysis, we identify predictive markers of PTC progression risk such as GPX3 and TMSB4X. Integration of clinical and proteomic data provides a valuable resource for  a deeper understanding of early-stage PTC biology and may inform personalized management strategies for patients with indolent or progressive disease.

papers.title: GENECraft: A Function- and Prior-Constrained Discrete Dynamical System for Controllable Regulatory DNA Design
papers.abstract: Designing regulatory DNA requires reconciling two complementary modeling paradigms: genomic language models (gLMs) capture evolutionary syntax without guaranteeing targeted regulatory activity, whereas sequence-to-function predictors provide explicit functional supervision without enforcing native-like sequence plausibility. We introduce GENECraft, a training-free Function- and Prior-Constrained Discrete Dynamical System (FP-DDS) that couples a genomic language model (Carbon) and a functional oracle (AlphaGenome) during inference-time optimization to balance predicted regulatory activity and consistency with genomic sequence priors. GENECraft evolves continuous latent nucleotide logits while evaluating strictly decoded discrete DNA sequences under a time-dependent composite vector field that fuses normalized functional utility, bidirectional contextual prior guidance, and compositional quality penalties, followed by feasibility-first trajectory readout. Across 2,185 loci spanning promoters, multi-constraint enhancers, and 18 transcription factors (TFs), GENECraft achieves full-joint success rates of 62.70%, 65.23%, and 94.56% (macro-averaged), substantially outperforming seven optimization, evolutionary, and generative baselines (which reach at most 2.15% on enhancers). In matched 336-locus ablations, in-loop Carbon guidance reduces native-relative dinucleotide divergence by 7.8--11.5%, enhancer context sensitivity by 10.5%, and TF mutation sensitivity by 11.0%, establishing FP-DDS as a principled framework for controllable regulatory DNA design.

papers.title: Leveraging the largest harmonized epigenomic data collection for metadata prediction validated and augmented over 350,000 public epigenomic datasets
papers.abstract: Epigenomic data found in public databases often suffer from issues of non-standardization and incompleteness in their associated metadata. There are currently no automated approaches to validate or correct such missing or inaccurate metadata information. To tackle this challenge, we harnessed the extensive harmonized data and metadata provided by the EpiATLAS project of the International Human Epigenome Consortium (IHEC) to train EpiClass, a suite of machine learning classifiers that can predict key metadata (~98% accuracy), including experimental assay, donor sex, biospecimen source and sample cancer status. The development of these classifiers enabled the identification of a few mislabeled and low-quality datasets in the EpiATLAS project, while also completing with high-confidence most of the missing metadata. These classifiers were also validated on thousands of ENCODE datasets absent from the initial training, then applied to assess more than 350,000 human ChIP-seq and RNA-seq datasets from public repositories. Overall, this effort not only validated the accuracy of the vast majority of assays reported by the original authors, but also unveiled ~500 datasets with discrepancies, in particular through data swap during data entry. More importantly, EpiClass also supplied high-confidence predictions for over 320,000 metadata attributes of the biological sample such as the sex, cancer status and biomaterial type, which had been originally omitted in the majority of cases. Our work introduces the first systematic approach for metadata correction and augmentation, enhancing the quality and reliability of publicly available epigenomic data.

papers.title: Machine Learning-based Transcriptomic Data Analysis of Long COVID Patients: Generating Hypotheses for Molecular Signatures
papers.abstract: Introduction: Long COVID (LC) remains a global public-health challenge, affecting an estimated 10-30% of COVID-19-survivors. Machine learning (ML) can help identify molecular features associated with LC. Human ion channels (HICs), that regulate immune-cell signaling and cellular homeostasis, may contribute to LC-associated processes and offer insights into relevant pathways and potential drug-repurposing candidates. Methodology: RNA-seq data from COVID-19-recovered and LC patients across six datasets were integrated, preprocessed, and corrected for batch effects. Supervised ML models were evaluated using leave-one-batch-out validation, with SHAP identifying features across validation folds. Functional enrichment, host-host and host-viral protein-protein interaction analyses were performed, followed by drug interaction analysis of potential HICs within the resulting interactome. Results: A support vector classifier with an RBF kernel achieved a mean-AUC of 0.664 across six validation folds. SHAP analysis of the three selected folds (AUC = 0.722, 0.836, and 0.817) identified 225, 153, and 241 genes, respectively. Functional enrichment highlighted pathways including histidine metabolism and TNF signaling. Among the 613 genes identified across these folds, 9 were HICs and 39 were immune signaling-related genes (ISGs), whose protein-protein interaction analysis revealed a pharmacologically relevant interactome. Furthermore, four HICs including CLCN3, KCNQ3, RYR1, and ZACN interacted with 30 approved drugs. Conclusion: ML-based analysis of integrated RNA-seq data identified HICs and ISGs associated with LC, while functional enrichment and PPI analyses provided insights into their potential biological relevance. Drug interaction analysis further highlighted candidate HIC-targeting drugs for future investigation in LC management. This computational framework provides preliminary, hypothesis-generating insights to guide future research.

papers.title: Dependence-Aware Conformal Prediction for 3D Uncertainty Quantification in Molecular Docking
papers.abstract: Molecular docking plays a critical role in drug discovery by predicting three-dimensional (3D) binding poses of small molecules within proteins. However, docking predictions can contain substantial positional errors, making reliable uncertainty quantification essential. Conformal prediction (CP) provides a principled framework for uncertainty quantification, yet constructing compact 3D prediction regions with reliable joint coverage remains challenging due to heterogeneous atomic errors, dependence among spatial coordinates, and distribution shifts. We develop a dependence-aware CP framework for molecular docking that leverages a shared graph neural network (GNN) to estimate adaptive, asymmetric uncertainty intervals using local atomic and global molecular information. Copula-based joint calibration accounts for dependence among coordinate-wise nonconformity scores to construct compact 3D prediction boxes. We further introduce density ratio estimation (DRE) to adapt calibration under distribution shift. Experiments across three docking methods demonstrate that our approach reduces median prediction-box volumes by 37.40%, 95.00%, and 39.16% for AutoDock Vina, Protenix, and MedusaGraph, respectively, compared with a state-of-the-art CP baseline, while achieving empirical joint coverage close to the 90% target. Under the Molecular Group Split and controlled distribution shifts, DRE further reduces coverage deviations, highlighting the potential of dependence-aware and shift-adaptive calibration for reliable 3D molecular docking uncertainty quantification.

papers.title: How predictable is an individual's DNA methylation?
papers.abstract: DNA methylation is largely shared among individuals of the same cell type, yet at specific genomic sites it differs substantially between individuals. Methods that predict methylation are usually evaluated by their accuracy over all sites. Because methylation at most sites is shared, this accuracy cannot show whether a method predicts an individual's methylation where individuals differ. We present individual-level methylation prediction at sites where individuals differ as a new challenge. Given the reference genome sequence, the methylation of other individuals of the same cell type, and measurements at some sites of a target individual, but not the individual's genotype, the task is to predict the target individual's methylation class (unmethylated, intermediate, or methylated) at the remaining sites. We evaluate predictions separately at sites with low and high variation across individuals. We compare four approaches: the average of other individuals, a sequence model (the DNA language model Nucleotide Transformer) fine-tuned on other individuals' methylation, the same model further fine-tuned on the target individual's measurements, and a local class-average approach using the target individual's nearby training-site class labels. Across 32 individuals from six human cell types, the average of other individuals matched or slightly exceeded both sequence models at sites with low variation among individuals. At the most variable sites, the average of other individuals performed worse than a random predictor that assigns classes at the observed class frequencies, whereas both sequence models performed substantially better than the average. Both sequence models also achieved higher mean weighted F1 than the local class-average approach. Fine-tuning on the target individual's measurements improved predictions more inside regions where other individuals show bimodal methylation (a mix of methylated and unmethylated DNA molecules within one sample) than outside them. Among the most variable sites, it also improved predictions at CpG islands for 25 of the 32 individuals. We conclude that individual-level methylation prediction is a distinct problem that is particularly challenging at sites where individuals differ, and that the benefit of an individual's own measurements is concentrated in genomic contexts identifiable from other individuals' methylation and genomic annotations.

papers.title: Deciphering Molecular Language for Spectral Interpretation with a Foundation Model Pretrained on Repository-Wide Metabolomics Data
papers.abstract: In-depth, scalable structural interpretation of tandem mass spectra from diverse biological tissues and environmental samples is essential for understanding the molecular diversity of cellular environments and the metabolic architecture of living systems. Although community-driven resources such as GNPS and MassIVE have aggregated massive volumes of tandem mass spectra spanning a wide range of organisms, clinical cohorts and environmental surveys, modeling and interpreting this exponentially expanding spectral corpus to distill molecular information and derive meaningful biological insights poses a fundamental challenge for established computational methods. Here we present UltraMS, a dual-polarity foundation model tailored to decipher the molecular language latent in tandem mass spectra through large-scale pretraining on more than 160 million spectra encompassing both positive and negative ion modes. Our findings illustrate that UltraMS is capable of effectively decoding the chemical semantics of molecules underlying mass spectra via self-supervised learning, achieving superior performance across a variety of downstream tasks, including elemental detection, molecular identification, molecular property profiling, and metabolic landscape characterization. Remarkably, UltraMS enables conducting molecular identification with fine-grained spectral interpretability, simultaneously elucidating molecular structures from untargeted MS/MS spectra and providing peak-by-peak substructural attributions via annotation transfer. Deployed on a clinical cohort of human plaque samples, UltraMS demonstrates significant potential in discovering previously unrecognized phenotype-linked metabolites supported by structurally grounded fragment-ion formation pathways, while effectively correcting likely misannotated clinical markers. Furthermore, building on the structure-aware spectral representations learned by UltraMS, we construct UltraAtlas, a chemical-property-resolved map that organizes millions of experimental spectra into a unified coordinate system, enabling millisecond-scale molecular profiling and offering practical guidance for exploratory navigation across vast chemical space. Applied to human scalp metabolomics, UltraAtlas effectively captures distinct metabolic variations across individuals, highlighting phenotype-specific chemical signatures while shedding light on the chemical niches of the resident microbiome. Together, UltraMS and UltraAtlas constitute a generalizable framework for structural elucidation and biological discovery from tandem mass spectra, empowering the comprehensive exploration of the largely undeciphered metabolomes across different domains of life.

papers.title: ModFormer: A unified structure-aware model of transcriptome-wide A-to-I RNA editing
papers.abstract: Adenosine-to-inosine (A-to-I) RNA editing can recode transcripts without permanently altering the genome. ADAR-catalyzed editing depends on both local sequence and RNA secondary structure, making it difficult to anticipate which sites will be edited or how mutations will change their activity. Moving from observing endogenous A-to-I editing to using it as a programmable molecular tool requires predicting how editing responds to sequence changes. Here, we present ModFormer, a model that integrates RNA sequence representations with predicted secondary structure to predict ADAR-mediated editing. Trained on human data, ModFormer predicts editing sites and rates across substrates and species unseen during training, recovers established sequence and pairing preferences, and anticipates experimentally measured responses to RNA mutations. These predictions prioritize responsive sites in mutational screens and guide an autonomous AI agent toward candidate RNA designs. ModFormer provides a framework for predicting how sequence changes reshape RNA editing and can be adapted to new substrates with limited experimental data.

papers.title: The PD-L1 metabolic interactome in glioma is bounded by IDH1 genotype
papers.abstract: Immune checkpoint blockade has failed in glioblastoma, and part of the reason may lie in the tumour cell itself: if the checkpoint and the metabolism that sustains the cell hold each other up, then lowering one arm hands the tumour the other, and a single agent cannot win. We tested that possibility in GL261 glioma cells of IDH1-wildtype and IDH1-mutant genotype, silencing Chka or Cd274, blocking PD-L1 with an antibody, and reading the consequences by RT-qPCR, RNA sequencing, flow cytometry of surface PD-L1 and high-resolution 1H NMR of dual-phase cell extracts. The two genes proved reciprocal in both genotypes: silencing either transcript raised the other, and silencing choline kinase roughly doubled PD-L1 at the cell surface. Antibody blockade did something the silencing did not. In IDH1-wildtype cells it lowered soluble phosphocholine, the only one of twenty-two aqueous signals to survive correction for multiple testing, and raised total lipid per cell without changing lipid composition, whereas silencing PD-L1 raised phosphocholine instead; in IDH1-mutant cells neither change occurred. The transcriptome drew the same boundary, engaging a sterol programme and lowering glycolysis, the tricarboxylic acid cycle and oxidative phosphorylation in wild-type cells only. The interferon response did not respect that boundary and rose under every perturbation in both genotypes. Removing PD-L1 from inside the cell and blocking it from outside are therefore not the same intervention, and the metabolic half of the response stops at the IDH1 genotype.

papers.title: Towards a Physiologically Rigorous Heartbeat Dynamics Foundation Model
papers.abstract: Capturing long-range heartbeat dynamics accurately from wearable electrocardiogram (ECG) recordings is a key challenge in personalized healthcare and autonomic neuroscience. Although classical methods are physiologically grounded and statistically rigorous, they cannot learn across population data and therefore cannot scale. Time series foundation models, on the other hand, can scale, but fail to capture physiologically meaningful beat-to-beat dynamics. We present, to our knowledge, the first probabilistic foundation model of heartbeat dynamics: a density-based neural temporal point process (NTPP) pretrained on RR-interval sequences from 11,226 subjects across five public datasets spanning normal sinus rhythm, arrhythmia, atrial fibrillation, and ischemia. We establish a physiological scaling law in this domain, showing that held-out metrics improve predictably with cohort size. We additionally show that scaling behavior in stochastic output domains like physiology should be evaluated by distributional calibration metrics (KS distance, goodness-of-fit) rather than point-error (MAE, RMSE), because point errors approach their irreducible floor while distributional properties continue to improve. Our pretrained model transfers zero-shot to a held-out ambulatory dataset, reaching 94.7% goodness-of-fit with no subject-specific data. In 5-minute autoregressive simulation, the model remains calibrated (87-88% goodness-of-fit) and generates trajectories with real physiological variability. Finally, we show that the learned representations are physiologically interpretable. The recurrent history embeddings separate normal and arrhythmia windows in held-out test subjects with a balanced accuracy of 95.7%. The lognormal mixture distributions show that arrhythmia subjects differ mainly in predictive spread (3.5x larger standard deviation than normal cohort), with only a small shift toward shorter mean RR than the normal group (0.79 vs. 0.86s). These results establish population-scale pretraining as a foundation for physiologically grounded modeling and simulation of heartbeat dynamics.

papers.title: All-Atom Structure Tokenizer: AtomLM-9b for Biomolecular Structure Prediction
papers.abstract: We develop an All-atom Structure Tokenizer that compresses biomolecular geometry into discrete structural tokens and achieves high-accuracy all-atom reconstruction. A hierarchical geometric encoder and finite scalar quantization map chemical units to a shared vocabulary of 8,192 tokens, while a joint coordinate de-tokenizer reconstructs backbone, side-chain, nucleic-acid, and ligand heavy atoms. The tokenizer achieves all-atom lDDT scores of 0.832 and 0.835 on CASP14 and CASP15, respectively. Building on this tokenizer, we train AtomLM-9b, an autoregressive language model based on Qwen3.5-9B that predicts structural tokens from molecular identities and connectivity and decodes them into complete atomic structures. We demonstrate, for the first time, protein structure prediction performance comparable to AlphaFold 3 with an all-atom-tokenizer-based structural language model: on the FoldBench protein-protein task, AtomLM-9b achieves a success rate of 75.01%, compared with the published AlphaFold 3 result of 72.93%. These results establish discrete all-atom tokenization as an effective interface between high-fidelity atomic reconstruction and language-model-based structure prediction.

papers.title: The antitumor peptide CIGB-552 is active in B-cell lymphomas and enhances BTK-targeted therapies
papers.abstract: Despite advances in targeted therapies, acquired resistance remains a major challenge in B-cell lymphomas. CIGB-552 is a synthetic antitumor peptide that modulates COMMD1-associated signaling pathways, but its activity in hematological malignancies remains unexplored. We investigated CIGB-552 in marginal zone lymphoma (MZL), mantle cell lymphoma (MCL), and diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) models, focusing on drug-resistant MZL and combinations with BTK-targeted agents. CIGB-552 reduced viability across lymphoma cell lines, with the greatest sensitivity in MZL and MCL, and retained activity in MZL models with acquired resistance to BTK, PI3K, or BCL2 inhibitors, but not in non-neoplastic B-cells. Peptide uptake varied among models and correlated with sensitivity, whereas treatment induced context-dependent apoptotic and non-apoptotic cell death. Integrated transcriptomic and proteomic analyses in MZL cells identified reduced B-cell receptor, NF-{kappa}B, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, and MAPK signaling alongside induction of cellular stress-response programs. Immunoblotting supported the suppression of key survival proteins and showed increased COMMD1 abundance. CIGB-552 enhanced the activity of ibrutinib in parental and resistant MZL models, and in a canine DLBCL cell line, and showed favorable interactions with additional BTK inhibitors and a BTK degrader. CIGB-552 also inhibited growth in primary lymphoma samples, and its combination with ibrutinib increased activity in primary MZL cells. These preclinical findings support further investigation of CIGB-552 as a therapeutic candidate for B-cell lymphomas, particularly in combination with BTK-targeted agents.

papers.title: Multi-omics analysis reveals how the natural compound bostrycin induces iron starvation and ferroptosis
papers.abstract: The development of novel anticancer drugs remains urgent due to limited efficacy of existing therapies. Natural products are a rich source for discovery of anticancer agents, yet their mechanisms often remain elusive. Bostrycin, a fungal anthraquinone with broad cytotoxicity, is one such compound. Here, we combine global and nascent proteomics with metabolomics to elucidate the mechanism of bostrycin-induced cell death. We show that bostrycin induces ferroptosis, and use thermal proteome profiling to identify thioredoxin reductase 1 (TXNRD1), a key enzyme in glutathione metabolism and redox control, as bostrycin's primary direct target. Bostrycin triggered an iron starvation response and reduced iron-sulfur cluster-containing proteins, consistent with impaired cysteine availability. While the resulting iron overload likely triggered ferroptotic death, this coincided with broader disruption of redox balance, glutathione metabolism, and energy pathways. These findings establish bostrycin's mechanism of action and identify it as a ferroptosis-inducing agent acting distinctly from canonical inducers.

papers.title: Learning interpretable rules of protein binding from a trillion interactions
papers.abstract: Protein binders are invaluable as research tools and therapeutics, yet why some targets readily yield binders while others resist discovery remains poorly understood. Here we quantify this variability through more than 1,300 independent selections against 96 protein targets, experimentally surveying over one trillion protein-protein interactions. We find that binder density-the probability that a random protein variant binds a target is reproducible, varies by at least five orders of magnitude, and depends primarily on target identity rather than library design. To uncover the molecular determinants of binding, we develop an energy-based machine-learning model that learns pairwise interactions between target and binder residues from protein language model embeddings, and introduce a decomposition that resolves these interactions into interpretable feature-feature couplings. Strikingly, the features associated with binders are extensively shared across targets, whereas those associated with targets are largely unique. These features both recover established molecular recognition mechanisms and identify previously unrecognized interactions in natural proteins. Several of the newly predicted interactions are validated experimentally. Our findings establish a quantitative framework for binder discovery and reveal a shared, interpretable, and transferable molecular vocabulary for predicting protein-protein interactions.

papers.title: ProFORGE: a composable sequence structure dynamics workflow validated by mechanoprotein design
papers.abstract: Designing a protein to resist tension requires identifying the contacts that bear the load. We developed ProFORGE to track residues as a scaffold changes length and to select designs by steered molecular dynamics. Starting with the 56-residue GB1 domain, we generated 14,542 candidates using protein language models for scaffold expansion and fixed-backbone design for sequence refinement. Of 182 sequences that passed the initial screen in the final round, 19 also met the AlphaFold 3 confidence threshold. The number of backbone hydrogen bonds between the terminal strands correlated with mean peak force at both simulated pulling speeds (Spearman \ensuremath{\rho} = 0.83--0.85). Two 98-residue designs shared less than 10\% global sequence identity with wild-type GB1. In single-molecule magnetic-tweezers measurements, their most probable unfolding forces were 117.9 and 132.1~pN, or 5.5 and 5.8 times those of the wild-type domains measured on the same tethers.

papers.title: Adaptive Representations for Real-World Enzyme Optimization
papers.abstract: Protein fitness landscapes are highly rugged, giving rise to complex optimization landscapes. Bayesian optimization (BO) with Gaussian processes (GPs) is widely used in protein engineering for its sample efficiency and calibrated uncertainty estimates. Here, we study a joint fine-tuning framework of a protein language model (PLM) and a GP across enzyme fitness landscapes that span various distinct mutation regimes encountered in real-world engineering campaigns. Joint fine-tuning optimizes the PLM and GP parameters together in an uncertainty-calibrated manner, providing an adaptive representation that utilizes the information from previously acquired points in addition to the existing knowledge from pretraining. Across seven combinatorial enzyme landscapes, this approach yields a median relative improvement in top-5% coverage of 45% over one-hot encoding and 120% over mean-pooled static ESM-C embeddings. We further explore several new pooling strategies beyond standard mean pooling within the joint fine-tuning framework and show that mutation-site pooling, which localizes the representation to mutated residues, is the most consistent performer across all landscapes, outperforming both established baselines and alternative pooling schemes. Finally, we show that the finetuned approach makes more effective use of training-split information, yielding better coverage across test-split BO rounds. These results suggest that adapting the representation during a campaign, rather than fixing it in advance, is the better design choice for BO-guided enzyme engineering.

papers.title: Transient telomerase mRNA delivery extends the proliferative capacity of patient-derived Duchenne muscular dystrophy myogenic progenitors
papers.abstract: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is an X-linked disease, characterised by progressive skeletal and cardiac muscle degeneration and impaired regeneration. Repeated regenerative cycles contribute to muscle stem cell exhaustion, potentially driven by telomere shortening under chronic proliferative demand. Here, we tested whether transient delivery of hTERT mRNA can increase the relative telomere signal (Q-FISH) in patient-derived DMD myogenic progenitors (CD56+) and interstitial (CD56-) cells from two DMD donors, compared with one control donor. hTERT mRNA treatment increased the relative telomere signal and added 2 to 6 population doublings in DMD myogenic progenitors, whereas healthy donor cells showed no comparable benefit in proliferation. Exploratory transcriptomic analysis indicated genotype-associated differences in translation- and cell-cycle-related gene sets following hTERT treatment. Telomere elongation and improved proliferation were not accompanied by recovery of myogenic differentiation; no karyotypic abnormalities were detected under the conditions tested. By transiently increasing the proliferative output of dystrophic cells without genomic integration, this proof of concept provides a basis for further investigation of telomere-associated proliferative limits in DMD and a starting point for future regenerative approaches.

papers.title: Distance-stratified benchmarking of variant-effect predictors on β-lactamase deep mutational scanning data
papers.abstract: Mutations far from the active site of antibiotic-resistance enzymes can change resistance, but it is unclear what information predicts their effects. We asked how the performance of a protein language model (ESM2), a structure-based stability predictor (ThermoMPNN) and simple structural descriptors changes with distance from the catalytic residues, using deep mutational scanning data for the {beta}-lactamases TEM-1 (four assays) and VIM-2 (one assay). We measured Spearman correlation and AUROC within distance bins, with bootstrap intervals over positions. In TEM-1, ESM2 accuracy fell with distance (Stiffler assay: {rho} = 0.72 below 8 [A] and 0.42 beyond 20 [A]), while the stability score rose ({rho} = 0.41 to 0.70). Adding stability to a model of ESM2, solvent accessibility and neighbour count improved cross-validated {rho} by 0.02 below 8 [A] and 0.10 beyond 20 [A], and the combined model did not decline with distance. The pattern held across binning schemes, in a continuous-distance model, and when any one of five contiguous distal stretches was removed. Two TEM-1 assays are nearly duplicates, and the Deng assay was too noisy to be informative. VIM-2 has only seven positions beyond 20 [A] and showed no detectable trend within 20 [A], so it neither supports nor contradicts the TEM-1 pattern. Nine distal TEM-1 positions remained more sensitive than the models predicted. In TEM-1, predicted stability was more informative than the language model far from the catalytic site, and the language model was stronger near it. Distance-stratified reporting could add to variant-effect benchmarks. The study is exploratory and uses one structure and one phenotype per assay.

papers.title: Agonistic anti-CD40 monoclonal antibody improves the antitumor efficacy of a clinical chemo-immunotherapy regimen in a refractory mouse neuroblastoma model.
papers.abstract: Background: The current standard regimen for relapsed-refractory high-risk neuroblastoma (HR-NB) is the combination of chemotherapy agents -Temozolomide and Irinotecan - and anti-GD2 antibody dinutuximab (TIG). This treatment results in an overall response for ~40% of patients, but the remaining 60% are resistant to TIG. We hypothesized that agonistic anti-CD40 monoclonal antibody (aCD40), which activates antitumor NK cells and macrophages as we found in previous studies, will improve the efficacy of TIG. Aim: To test the combination of aCD40 and TIG in a mouse HR-NB model that is resistant to TIG. Methods: For these studies, we used a clinically relevant, immunologically cold, HR-NB murine model, 9464D-GD2. Syngeneic mice were intradermally injected with the tumor cells.
