When tumors were established, mice were randomized and treated with TIG and/or aCD40. Tumor growth and mouse survival were followed. Mice that rejected their tumors were rechallenged to test immunological memory. Changes in immune cells were evaluated by flow cytometry and single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNAseq). Results: Similar to ~60% of patients with relapsed/refractory HR-NB, mice bearing 9464D-GD2 tumors did not respond to TIG. Adding aCD40 to TIG induced complete tumor regression in most mice bearing small tumors and extended survival, with many mice remaining tumor-free. The combination of aCD40 and TIG was more effective than aCD40 alone. The antitumor effect of TIG+aCD40 was not inhibited in T cell- or neutrophil-depleted mice but was substantially reduced in NK cell- and macrophage-depleted mice, indicating a role for both NK cells and macrophages in the antitumor effect. Involvement of these cells was consistent with flow cytometry and scRNAseq analyses. Mice treated with TIG+aCD40 that remained tumor-free were rechallenged with 9464D-GD2 cells and showed significantly reduced tumor growth compared to naive mice, indicating a memory response. This memory response was reduced in T cell-depleted mice, indicating the involvement of T cells in memory. Conclusion: These results show that while TIG alone was ineffective, a combination of aCD40 and TIG induced substantial tumor eradication in the 9464D-GD2 tumor model, suggesting that aCD40 may warrant future testing as an addition to the current standard TIG regimen for children with relapsed-refractory HR-NB.

papers.title: RecurSieve: A Python Package to Detect Subtle Gene Expression Differences Across Single-Cell RNA-seq Comparisons Using Iterative Machine Learning
papers.abstract: Most existing methods for performing differential expression testing using single-cell RNA-seq data evaluate genes independently and primarily detect shifts in mean RNA levels. These methods may thus miss RNAs that distinguish experimental groups jointly or through changes in the shape of genes' expression distributions. To address this limitation, we developed RecurSieve, an iterative ensemble learning method that combines shared expression classification with unsupervised clustering to recursively identify gene sets with group-based expression differences. Because experimental labels apply to heterogeneous populations of single cells within each comparative group, RecurSieve allows dynamic label reassignment during iterative training to detect subtle, non-linear expression patterns. In benchmarking experiments using simulated data with staged distributional expression differences, RecurSieve recovered more genes (2.3-3.9 of 10 staged genes) across groups as compared to standard methods (Wilcoxon, t-test, and logistic regression; 0.0-0.7 staged genes). When applied to a single nuclei RNA-seq analysis containing low and high-pathology stages of Alzheimer's disease (46 human donor brains), RecurSieve extended results from standard approaches by identifying genes including WWOX, DPP10, KCNIP4, HS6ST3, and CNTN5 which tend to exhibit stage-specific distributional expression differences accompanied by only minor changes in average expression. A subset of the genes exclusively detected in RecurSieve analysis had been previously associated with Alzheimer's disease, underscoring the potential importance resulting from the unique sensitivity of our method. These simulated and empirical single-cell RNA-seq results demonstrate how the RecurSieve framework complements standard methods for identifying genes with unique group-specific expression differences independent of changes in average expression.

papers.title: Microdomes: Micro-engineered Microdome arrays enable standardised and shear-free 3D biology with full-spectrum optical imaging compatibility
papers.abstract: Three-dimensional cellular models such as organoids and spheroids hold major promise for developmental biology, disease modelling and precision medicine, yet their large-scale production and analysis remain constrained by handling-induced shear stress, sample fragility, positional instability and limited compatibility with advanced imaging workflows. Here, we introduce Microdomes, dense arrays of open-top, dome-shaped microcavities. Each cavity holds a single specimen in its own miniature aquarium, accessed through a narrow apical opening that admits cells, medium, matrix and staining reagents while shielding it from the shear generated during routine pipetting. Each Microdomes chip accommodates more than 100 spheroids or organoids, supporting diverse cell types, co-culture formats and both matrix-free and matrix-embedded culture. All specimens are retained through prolonged culture, repeated medium exchange, fixation and immunostaining. Because every specimen occupies a fixed, addressable position against a thin transparent film, the same spheroid can be relocated and re-imaged over weeks of culture and across microscopes, from array-wide overviews to subcellular details, without transfer, embedding or other perturbation. Microdomes also support AI-based automated segmentation, from whole-spheroid outlines to individual nuclei in 3D, using common image analysis software. Microdomes thereby turn each array into a self-contained quality control unit, providing specimen-level traceability that organoid production pipelines currently lack.

papers.title: Distill-Mol: Learning unified molecular representations via cross-modal fusion and hierarchical geometric distillation
papers.abstract: Molecular representation learning aims to link molecular structures to downstream tasks in drug discovery and materials design. Molecules contain multi-level information, including semantic, topological, and geometric features. However, existing methods often rely on single-modality representations or shallow fusion strategies, limiting their ability to capture complex structure-property relationships. To address this issue, this paper proposes Distill-Mol, a multimodal molecular representation learning framework that formulates molecular representation learning as a language-structure-physics (LSP) collaborative modeling problem. Distill-Mol aligns SMILES semantics, molecular topology, and three-dimensional geometric information in a shared representation space and transfers geometric knowledge from a teacher trained with conformation angle noise to a student trained with coordinate Gaussian noise, enhancing geometric consistency and structural interpretability. In the fusion stage, cross-modal interaction and adaptive gating integrate complementary semantic, topological, and geometric information into task-adaptive molecular representations. Experimental results on MoleculeNet and QM9 demonstrate that Distill-Mol achieves competitive performance across diverse molecular prediction tasks. Additional experiments on DTA and DTI benchmarks further evaluate its applicability to biomedical interaction prediction. Ablation studies, perturbation validation, and interpretability analyses show that Distill-Mol learns task-relevant multimodal representations, improving predictive performance, robustness, and structural interpretability.

papers.title: A Reproducible, Leakage-Aware Machine Learning Pipeline for Antimicrobial Peptide Activity Prediction
papers.abstract: Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) are key alternatives to conventional antibiotics, but published machine learning models may overestimate predictive performance because of positive-class sequence redundancy and data leakage. We developed a leakage-aware pipeline using 13,469 peptides from DRAMP v5.0 and UniProt, clustered at 40% sequence identity with CD-HIT to enforce cluster-level splitting. A Random Forest trained on sequence and physicochemical features achieved an AUC-ROC of 0.939 and a Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) of 0.671 on a cluster-disjoint test set (mean AUC-ROC 0.923 {+/-} 0.012 across 20 repeated cluster-disjoint splits, versus 0.945 {+/-} 0.004 under random splitting). Adding ESMFold-derived structural features did not improve aggregate metrics; a diagnostic analysis that separated directly folded from propagated sequences, and examined a length confound, showed a small positive difference (+0.010 AUC, not tested for significance) on directly folded sequences and a small negative difference (-0.007) on sequences with propagated features. SHAP analysis identified net cationic charge as the primary driver of predictions, consistent with known membrane-disruption mechanisms. Secondary classifiers of activity spectrum achieved AUC-ROCs of 0.871 (Gram-positive) and 0.851 (Gram-negative). Among 22 clinical-stage peptides with no exact-sequence match in the training or test sets, the mean predicted probability was 0.73; a high score for the non-antibacterial amphipathic peptide enfuvirtide suggests that the features capture broad membrane-interaction traits rather than antibacterial specificity. The pipeline is implemented as an open-source, 29-rule Snakemake workflow.

papers.title: Continually pretrained open-weight language models can outperform traditional machine learning in EHR-based clinical prediction
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) prompted with electronic health record (EHR) data have predicted clinical outcomes less accurately than locally trained machine-learning models. We developed VEX-EHR by extending the vocabulary of a 12-billion-parameter open-weight LLM (weights publicly available) with 17,601 clinical and audit-log codes from 170,483 patients records at one academic medical center, continuing its pretraining on those 2019-2024 records (4.7 billion tokens) and fine-tuning it per task. AUROCs were 0.917 for next-24-hour discharge, 0.715 for 30-day readmission and 0.847 for intensive care unit acute kidney injury, against 0.868, 0.677 and 0.828 for gradient-boosted trees and 0.848, 0.650 and 0.791 for CEHR-BERT, an EHR foundation model. Continued pretraining added 0.031-0.053 AUROC on every task. With 10% of the labels, VEX-EHR exceeded both comparators using all labels for discharge, and CEHR-BERT for readmission, valuable where labels are costly. Adapted by continued pretraining, open-weight LLMs can outperform traditional machine learning in EHR-based prediction.

papers.title: Integrated real-world and translational studies nominate CREB binding protein/EP3001 inhibition to overcome androgen receptor pathway modulator resistance in men with prostate cancer
papers.abstract: Androgen pathway modulators (APMs) have significantly improved outcomes for men with metastatic prostate cancer, but the evolution of therapy resistance is nearly universal, and there remains a major clinical need to identify actionable vulnerabilities for therapy-resistant disease. To address this need, we employed regulatory network models that leverage multi-omic data from over 10,000 prostate cancer patients with longitudinal clinical data. Analysis of the architecture of the network models identified EP300 as the top actionable target associated with androgen receptor-mediated therapy resistance. These observations were validated using a novel inhibitor of CBP/EP300, pocenbrodib, which showed preclinical activity in vitro and in vivo. Acetylomics analysis and functional studies pinpointed inhibition of oxidative phosphorylation and fatty acid metabolism as key mechanisms of action for pocenbrodib. Clinical benefit for this agent was demonstrated in a patient with metastatic APM-resistant prostate cancer (NCT04575766), highlighting CBP/EP300 as a key target for further translation.

papers.title: LifeLine.ai: A SigLIP-MedGemma Multimodal Framework with KTO Alignment for Open-Vocabulary 12-Lead ECG Report Generation
papers.abstract: Automated twelve-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) interpretation has historically relied on discriminative classifiers limited to closed-set diagnostic labels, signal reconstruction, or saliency heatmaps. While categorizing predefined arrhythmias well, these static classifiers cannot generate narrative clinical reports, incorporate patient history, or support interactive clinical question-answering (Q&A). We present LifeLine.ai, an end-toend multimodal Vision-ECG-Language framework for automated cardiac diagnosis and clinical reporting. After early attempts at waveform peak-tracking and coordinate mapping failed against complex morphological variations, we leveraged large-scale PhysioNet repositories (MIMIC-IV and PTB-XL). Because hardware limits precluded training on over 800,000 raw records, we curated a balanced subset to estimate performance, converting one-dimensional signals into 3x4 twelve-lead grids with continuous Lead II rhythm strips at the bottom. Our pipeline integrates YOLOv11s localization, a LoRAadapted Google SigLIP encoder, a trainable Multi-Layer Perceptron projector, and a 4-bit quantized MedGemma-4B model, complemented by a separate Kahneman-Tversky Optimization (KTO) pipeline built on collected user feedback and a multi-LLM consensus engine. On this compact subset, SigLIP outperformed Swin Transformer encodings (~0.21 vs. ~0.25 validation loss), achieving 71.0% open-vocabulary precision and a 75.0% contextual F1 score across a cloud deployment spanning Vercel, mobile apps, Amazon EC2, Firebase, Hugging Face, Modal GPUs, and lifelinecg-sdk. Our code is available at https://github.com/Asad939asad/ LifeLine.ai-.

papers.title: Benchmarking Protein Structure Tokenizers as Generation Targets for Language Models
papers.abstract: Discrete structure tokenizers are the standard way to give a language model access to protein three-dimensional structure, yet they are selected on how accurately they can be read, their reconstruction fidelity, while the property that governs generation is how well a model can write them. We measure this property, writability, directly: holding the base model, data, recipe and compute fixed, we swap only the tokenizer and train the same 9B model to emit structure tokens residue by residue, over eight tokenizers, four compute budgets and three evaluation sets (96 cells). At 2B tokens final writability runs from TM 0.662 down to 0.378 under identical conditions, with five of the eight arms clearing the TM 0.5 mark at which a fold is usually called correct and three falling short of it. Neither codebook size nor reconstruction ceiling explains where an arm lands; the best and worst both use 8192 codewords. What does explain the spread is local structure preservation of the code space. In DPLM-2 a one-bit codeword error costs 0.019 TM where a random codeword costs 0.347, and the trained model's own errors are correspondingly local, at 0.51 of the random Hamming expectation; FoldToken4 fails both tests at the same codebook size and is 0.13 TM less writable. Three controls discipline how such a benchmark may be read. A same-recipe rerun puts the noise floor at $σ=0.0067$ TM, which collapses an apparent six-way ranking into four tiers. A reference-free geometry panel turns out to be nearly orthogonal to TM (Pearson $-0.58$), with the worst arm by TM producing the most physically valid backbones. And two pre-registered interventions are null for a reason the mechanism measurements reveal: the quantity they target saturates at 1.5B tokens while TM is still rising. All 131 evaluation cells, including raw generated token streams, are released.

papers.title: Learning Multimodal Representations from Partially Paired, Small-Scale Data
papers.abstract: Modeling multimodal data from partially paired samples is critical for advancing domains like biomedicine, where vast unimodal datasets and foundation models exist but paired data remains scarce. Existing fusion methods rely on large-scale paired datasets, limiting their use in scenarios with incomplete pairing. We introduce CAMEO, an adversarial learning-based modality fusion framework that integrates modalities from small, partially paired datasets. Combining any pre-trained unimodal encoder with a cross-modal latent alignment mechanism, CAMEO learns shared representations requiring only minimal paired samples. Evaluated on computational pathology tasks such as niche classification and cell type composition prediction, CAMEO achieves superior data efficiency, outperforming contrastive approaches like CLIP in low paired-data regimes, and highlighting the benefits of adversarial alignment when paired annotations are scarce. To facilitate further research, we additionally release a fully annotated HuggingFace dataset comprising three organs and paired image and gene expression modalities. By extending fusion methods to address limited pairing and small-scale datasets, we provide a framework that advances multimodal learning and broadens its applicability to real-world biomedical problems.

papers.title: RumiFold: Teaching an LLM to Natively Fold Proteins and Reason About Their Function
papers.abstract: Can we teach a general-purpose language model to fold proteins? And if so, what does learning to fold enable beyond structure prediction itself? We introduce RumiFold, a pretrained chat model that learns to predict protein structures directly from its own hidden states. RumiFold processes proteins through repeated folding passes, then uses these folded representations to answer questions in natural language. It achieves folding accuracy comparable to dedicated single-representation models such as SimpleFold, alongside state-of-the-art performance on Gene Ontology protein function prediction and free-text function description. We find that folding pretraining organizes the model's hidden states around protein function, creating an internal per-residue workspace that is biologically grounded. Causal interventions show that this folded workspace links structure and language when RumiFold predicts function, providing rich representations for biomolecular reasoning. We see RumiFold as a step toward native biomolecular intelligence: where protein-based computations and language-based reasoning become integrated capabilities of general-purpose language models. Code, data, and models are available at: https://rumifold.baulab.info

papers.title: Solo: Doublet Identification in Single-Cell RNA-Seq via Semi-Supervised Deep Learning
papers.abstract: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) measurements of gene expression enable an unprecedented high-resolution view into cellular state. However, current methods often result in two or more cells that share the same cell-identifying barcode; these "doublets" violate the fundamental premise of single-cell technology and can lead to incorrect inferences. Here, we describe Solo, a semi-supervised deep learning approach that identifies doublets with greater accuracy than existing methods. Solo embeds cells unsupervised using a variational autoencoder and then appends a feed-forward neural network layer to the encoder to form a supervised classifier. We train this classifier to distinguish simulated doublets from the observed data. Solo can be applied in combination with experimental doublet detection methods to further purify scRNA-seq data to true single cells. It is freely available from https://github.com/calico/solo. A record of this paper's transparent peer review process is included in the Supplemental Information.

papers.title: Generating 3D molecules conditional on receptor binding sites with deep generative models
papers.abstract: The goal of structure-based drug discovery is to find small molecules that bind to a given target protein. Deep learning has been used to generate drug-like molecules with certain cheminformatic properties, but has not yet been applied to generating 3D molecules predicted to bind to proteins by sampling the conditional distribution of protein-ligand binding interactions. In this work, we describe for the first time a deep learning system for generating 3D molecular structures conditioned on a receptor binding site. We approach the problem using a conditional variational autoencoder trained on an atomic density grid representation of cross-docked protein-ligand structures. We apply atom fitting and bond inference procedures to construct valid molecular conformations from generated atomic densities. We evaluate the properties of the generated molecules and demonstrate that they change significantly when conditioned on mutated receptors. We also explore the latent space learned by our generative model using sampling and interpolation techniques. This work opens the door for end-to-end prediction of stable bioactive molecules from protein structures with deep learning.

papers.title: Deep generative modeling of sample-level heterogeneity in single-cell genomics
papers.abstract: Single-cell genomic studies were recently conducted on hundred of samples exhibiting complex designs. These data have tremendous potential for discovering how sample- or tissue-level phenotypes relate to cellular and molecular composition. However, current analyses are often based on simplified representations of these data by averaging information across cells. We present multi-resolution variational inference (MrVI), a deep generative model designed to realize the potential of cohort studies at the single-cell level. MrVI tackles two fundamental, intertwined problems: stratifying samples into groups and evaluating the cellular and molecular differences between groups, without requiring predefined cell states. Leveraging its single-cell perspective, MrVI detects clinically relevant stratifications of cohorts of people with COVID-19 or inflammatory bowel disease that are manifested in only certain cellular subsets, enabling new discoveries that would otherwise be overlooked. MrVI can de novo identify groups of small molecules with similar biochemical properties and evaluate their effects on cellular composition and gene expression in large-scale perturbation studies. MrVI is an open-source tool at scvi-tools.org .

papers.title: ACTINN: automated identification of cell types in single cell RNA sequencing
papers.abstract: Abstract Motivation Cell type identification is one of the major goals in single cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq). Current methods for assigning cell types typically involve the use of unsupervised clustering, the identification of signature genes in each cluster, followed by a manual lookup of these genes in the literature and databases to assign cell types. However, there are several limitations associated with these approaches, such as unwanted sources of variation that influence clustering and a lack of canonical markers for certain cell types. Here, we present ACTINN (Automated Cell Type Identification using Neural Networks), which employs a neural network with three hidden layers, trains on datasets with predefined cell types and predicts cell types for other datasets based on the trained parameters. Results We trained the neural network on a mouse cell type atlas (Tabula Muris Atlas) and a human immune cell dataset, and used it to predict cell types for mouse leukocytes, human PBMCs and human T cell sub types. The results showed that our neural network is fast and accurate, and should therefore be a useful tool to complement existing scRNA-seq pipelines. Availability and implementation The codes and datasets are available at https://figshare.com/articles/ACTINN/8967116. Tutorial is available at https://github.com/mafeiyang/ACTINN. All codes are implemented in python. Supplementary information Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.

papers.title: Folding non-homologous proteins by coupling deep-learning contact maps with I-TASSER assembly simulations
papers.abstract: Structure prediction for proteins lacking homologous templates in the Protein Data Bank (PDB) remains a significant unsolved problem. We developed a protocol, C-I-TASSER, to integrate interresidue contact maps from deep neural-network learning with the cutting-edge I-TASSER fragment assembly simulations. Large-scale benchmark tests showed that C-I-TASSER can fold more than twice the number of non-homologous proteins than the I-TASSER, which does not use contacts. When applied to a folding experiment on 8,266 unsolved Pfam families, C-I-TASSER successfully folded 4,162 domain families, including 504 folds that are not found in the PDB. Furthermore, it created correct folds for 85% of proteins in the SARS-CoV-2 genome, despite the quick mutation rate of the virus and sparse sequence profiles. The results demonstrated the critical importance of coupling whole-genome and metagenome-based evolutionary information with optimal structure assembly simulations for solving the problem of non-homologous protein structure prediction.

papers.title: THItoGene: a deep learning method for predicting spatial transcriptomics from histological images
papers.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics unveils the complex dynamics of cell regulation and transcriptomes, but it is typically cost-prohibitive. Predicting spatial gene expression from histological images via artificial intelligence offers a more affordable option, yet existing methods fall short in extracting deep-level information from pathological images. In this paper, we present THItoGene, a hybrid neural network that utilizes dynamic convolutional and capsule networks to adaptively sense potential molecular signals in histological images for exploring the relationship between high-resolution pathology image phenotypes and regulation of gene expression. A comprehensive benchmark evaluation using datasets from human breast cancer and cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma has demonstrated the superior performance of THItoGene in spatial gene expression prediction. Moreover, THItoGene has demonstrated its capacity to decipher both the spatial context and enrichment signals within specific tissue regions. THItoGene can be freely accessed at https://github.com/yrjia1015/THItoGene.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence in Oncology: Current Capabilities, Future Opportunities, and Ethical Considerations
papers.abstract: The promise of highly personalized oncology care using artificial intelligence (AI) technologies has been forecasted since the emergence of the field. Cumulative advances across the science are bringing this promise to realization, including refinement of machine learning- and deep learning algorithms; expansion in the depth and variety of databases, including multiomics; and the decreased cost of massively parallelized computational power. Examples of successful clinical applications of AI can be found throughout the cancer continuum and in multidisciplinary practice, with computer vision-assisted image analysis in particular having several U.S. Food and Drug Administration-approved uses. Techniques with emerging clinical utility include whole blood multicancer detection from deep sequencing, virtual biopsies, natural language processing to infer health trajectories from medical notes, and advanced clinical decision support systems that combine genomics and clinomics. Substantial issues have delayed broad adoption, with data transparency and interpretability suffering from AI's "black box" mechanism, and intrinsic bias against underrepresented persons limiting the reproducibility of AI models and perpetuating health care disparities. Midfuture projections of AI maturation involve increasing a model's complexity by using multimodal data elements to better approximate an organic system. Far-future positing includes living databases that accumulate all aspects of a person's health into discrete data elements; this will fuel highly convoluted modeling that can tailor treatment selection, dose determination, surveillance modality and schedule, and more. The field of AI has had a historical dichotomy between its proponents and detractors. The successful development of recent applications, and continued investment in prospective validation that defines their impact on multilevel outcomes, has established a momentum of accelerated progress.
papers.venue: American Society of Clinical Oncology Educational Book

papers.title: Spatial cellular architecture predicts prognosis in glioblastoma
papers.abstract: Intra-tumoral heterogeneity and cell-state plasticity are key drivers for the therapeutic resistance of glioblastoma. Here, we investigate the association between spatial cellular organization and glioblastoma prognosis. Leveraging single-cell RNA-seq and spatial transcriptomics data, we develop a deep learning model to predict transcriptional subtypes of glioblastoma cells from histology images. Employing this model, we phenotypically analyze 40 million tissue spots from 410 patients and identify consistent associations between tumor architecture and prognosis across two independent cohorts. Patients with poor prognosis exhibit higher proportions of tumor cells expressing a hypoxia-induced transcriptional program. Furthermore, a clustering pattern of astrocyte-like tumor cells is associated with worse prognosis, while dispersion and connection of the astrocytes with other transcriptional subtypes correlate with decreased risk. To validate these results, we develop a separate deep learning model that utilizes histology images to predict prognosis. Applying this model to spatial transcriptomics data reveal survival-associated regional gene expression programs. Overall, our study presents a scalable approach to unravel the transcriptional heterogeneity of glioblastoma and establishes a critical connection between spatial cellular architecture and clinical outcomes.

papers.title: Integrated analysis of multimodal single-cell data with structural similarity
papers.abstract: Multimodal single-cell sequencing technologies provide unprecedented information on cellular heterogeneity from multiple layers of genomic readouts. However, joint analysis of two modalities without properly handling the noise often leads to overfitting of one modality by the other and worse clustering results than vanilla single-modality analysis. How to efficiently utilize the extra information from single cell multi-omics to delineate cell states and identify meaningful signal remains as a significant computational challenge. In this work, we propose a deep learning framework, named SAILERX, for efficient, robust, and flexible analysis of multi-modal single-cell data. SAILERX consists of a variational autoencoder with invariant representation learning to correct technical noises from sequencing process, and a multimodal data alignment mechanism to integrate information from different modalities. Instead of performing hard alignment by projecting both modalities to a shared latent space, SAILERX encourages the local structures of two modalities measured by pairwise similarities to be similar. This strategy is more robust against overfitting of noises, which facilitates various downstream analysis such as clustering, imputation, and marker gene detection. Furthermore, the invariant representation learning part enables SAILERX to perform integrative analysis on both multi- and single-modal datasets, making it an applicable and scalable tool for more general scenarios.

papers.title: DeepTCR is a deep learning framework for revealing sequence concepts within T-cell repertoires
papers.abstract: Deep learning algorithms have been utilized to achieve enhanced performance in pattern-recognition tasks. The ability to learn complex patterns in data has tremendous implications in immunogenomics. T-cell receptor (TCR) sequencing assesses the diversity of the adaptive immune system and allows for modeling its sequence determinants of antigenicity. We present DeepTCR, a suite of unsupervised and supervised deep learning methods able to model highly complex TCR sequencing data by learning a joint representation of a TCR by its CDR3 sequences and V/D/J gene usage. We demonstrate the utility of deep learning to provide an improved 'featurization' of the TCR across multiple human and murine datasets, including improved classification of antigen-specific TCRs and extraction of antigen-specific TCRs from noisy single-cell RNA-Seq and T-cell culture-based assays. Our results highlight the flexibility and capacity for deep neural networks to extract meaningful information from complex immunogenomic data for both descriptive and predictive purposes.

papers.title: DNABERT-S: pioneering species differentiation with species-aware DNA embeddings
papers.abstract: SUMMARY: We introduce DNABERT-S, a tailored genome model that develops species-aware embeddings to naturally cluster and segregate DNA sequences of different species in the embedding space. Differentiating species from genomic sequences (i.e. DNA and RNA) is vital yet challenging, since many real-world species remain uncharacterized, lacking known genomes for reference. Embedding-based methods are therefore used to differentiate species in an unsupervised manner. DNABERT-S builds upon a pre-trained genome foundation model named DNABERT-2. To encourage effective embeddings to error-prone long-read DNA sequences, we introduce Manifold Instance Mixup (MI-Mix), a contrastive objective that mixes the hidden representations of DNA sequences at randomly selected layers and trains the model to recognize and differentiate these mixed proportions at the output layer. We further enhance it with the proposed Curriculum Contrastive Learning (C2LR) strategy. Empirical results on 28 diverse datasets show DNABERT-S's effectiveness, especially in realistic label-scarce scenarios. For example, it identifies twice more species from a mixture of unlabeled genomic sequences, doubles the Adjusted Rand Index (ARI) in species clustering, and outperforms the top baseline's performance in 10-shot species classification with just a 2-shot training. AVAILABILITY AND IMPLEMENTATION: Model, codes, and data are publically available at https://github.com/MAGICS-LAB/DNABERT_S.

papers.title: De novo design of protein structure and function with RFdiffusion
papers.abstract: There has been considerable recent progress in designing new proteins using deep-learning methods 1–9 . Despite this progress, a general deep-learning framework for protein design that enables solution of a wide range of design challenges, including de novo binder design and design of higher-order symmetric architectures, has yet to be described. Diffusion models 10,11 have had considerable success in image and language generative modelling but limited success when applied to protein modelling, probably due to the complexity of protein backbone geometry and sequence–structure relationships. Here we show that by fine-tuning the RoseTTAFold structure prediction network on protein structure denoising tasks, we obtain a generative model of protein backbones that achieves outstanding performance on unconditional and topology-constrained protein monomer design, protein binder design, symmetric oligomer design, enzyme active site scaffolding and symmetric motif scaffolding for therapeutic and metal-binding protein design. We demonstrate the power and generality of the method, called RoseTTAFold diffusion (RFdiffusion), by experimentally characterizing the structures and functions of hundreds of designed symmetric assemblies, metal-binding proteins and protein binders. The accuracy of RFdiffusion is confirmed by the cryogenic electron microscopy structure of a designed binder in complex with influenza haemagglutinin that is nearly identical to the design model. In a manner analogous to networks that produce images from user-specified inputs, RFdiffusion enables the design of diverse functional proteins from simple molecular specifications.

papers.title: Robust deep learning–based protein sequence design using ProteinMPNN
papers.abstract: Although deep learning has revolutionized protein structure prediction, almost all experimentally characterized de novo protein designs have been generated using physically based approaches such as Rosetta. Here, we describe a deep learning–based protein sequence design method, ProteinMPNN, that has outstanding performance in both in silico and experimental tests. On native protein backbones, ProteinMPNN has a sequence recovery of 52.4% compared with 32.9% for Rosetta. The amino acid sequence at different positions can be coupled between single or multiple chains, enabling application to a wide range of current protein design challenges. We demonstrate the broad utility and high accuracy of ProteinMPNN using x-ray crystallography, cryo–electron microscopy, and functional studies by rescuing previously failed designs, which were made using Rosetta or AlphaFold, of protein monomers, cyclic homo-oligomers, tetrahedral nanoparticles, and target-binding proteins.

papers.title: DNABERT: pre-trained Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers model for DNA-language in genome
papers.abstract: MOTIVATION: Deciphering the language of non-coding DNA is one of the fundamental problems in genome research. Gene regulatory code is highly complex due to the existence of polysemy and distant semantic relationship, which previous informatics methods often fail to capture especially in data-scarce scenarios. RESULTS: To address this challenge, we developed a novel pre-trained bidirectional encoder representation, named DNABERT, to capture global and transferrable understanding of genomic DNA sequences based on up and downstream nucleotide contexts. We compared DNABERT to the most widely used programs for genome-wide regulatory elements prediction and demonstrate its ease of use, accuracy and efficiency. We show that the single pre-trained transformers model can simultaneously achieve state-of-the-art performance on prediction of promoters, splice sites and transcription factor binding sites, after easy fine-tuning using small task-specific labeled data. Further, DNABERT enables direct visualization of nucleotide-level importance and semantic relationship within input sequences for better interpretability and accurate identification of conserved sequence motifs and functional genetic variant candidates. Finally, we demonstrate that pre-trained DNABERT with human genome can even be readily applied to other organisms with exceptional performance. We anticipate that the pre-trained DNABERT model can be fined tuned to many other sequence analyses tasks. AVAILABILITY AND IMPLEMENTATION: The source code, pretrained and finetuned model for DNABERT are available at GitHub (https://github.com/jerryji1993/DNABERT). SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.

papers.title: Expanding antimicrobial chemical space by engineering drug safety.
papers.abstract: Antimicrobial-resistant (AMR) infections are a major health threat. Although advances in high-throughput screening, genome mining, and machine learning have accelerated antimicrobial discovery, insufficient separation between antibacterial efficacy and host toxicity remains a bottleneck to the clinical development of new antimicrobial compounds. Here, we establish a generalizable, two-component strategy to engineer drug safety and mobilize otherwise inaccessible chemical space for antimicrobial therapy, using calicheamicin, a potent cytotoxin with unacceptable host toxicity, as a proof of concept. First, we engineer a conditionally active drug conjugate that limits calicheamicin activity to infected tissue, thereby reducing systemic toxicity. Second, we engineer a self-resistance enzyme from Micromonospora echinospora, the natural producer of calicheamicin, as a long-circulating antidote to neutralize calicheamicin outside infected tissue, further reducing off-target toxicity. The conjugate exhibits activity against Gram-positive and Gram-negative pathogens upon exposure to a protease present within the infected microenvironment. When delivered with the antidote, antibacterial efficacy is maintained while off-target toxicity is reduced in mouse models of Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacterial pneumonia. We anticipate that our dual strategy, which engineers drug safety rather than selecting for it, provides a generalizable framework for mobilizing promising but toxic compounds as antimicrobials.

papers.title: MissenseDB: proteome-wide human missense variant effect prediction database with structural context.
papers.abstract: Missense variant-effect predictors now provide proteome-scale estimates of amino acid substitution impact, but their outputs remain distributed across independent resources and are difficult to explore jointly with protein structural and human-variation context. We present MissenseDB, a residue-centric database integrating three architecturally distinct transformer-based predictors, AlphaMissense, VESM-3B, and VESPA, across the reviewed human proteome. MissenseDB contains 10 734 339 residue positions across 19 436 canonical human proteins, with complete three-predictor coverage for 19 434 proteins. Predictor outputs are linked to 211 731 UniProt-to-structure mappings, residue-level secondary-structure and molecular-context annotations, and Pfam domain membership, together with 59 851 HUMSAVAR missense variants enriched with population allele frequencies and ClinVar annotations. Raw predictor scores are provided together with empirically calibrated probabilities referenced to a common prior, on which a single decision threshold applies; on this calibrated scale all three predictors agree on ~75%-77% of pathogenic and benign variants. An interactive interface couples protein-wide sequence tracks with three-dimensional structural visualization and provides access to the complete 19-substitution landscape at individual residues. REST endpoints support protein-, residue-, and proteome-scale retrieval, while versioned relational database snapshots and a genomic coordinate lookup table enabling direct mapping from GRCh38 VCF coordinates to UniProt residues enable reproducible bulk analysis. MissenseDB is freely accessible without registration at https://biosig.lab.uq.edu.au/missense_db.

papers.title: VEuPathDB: 2026 update on data, tools, and infrastructure for eukaryotic pathogens, vectors, and hosts.
papers.abstract: The eukaryotic pathogen, vector, and host informatics resource (VEuPathDB, https://veupathdb.org) provides open access to genomic and other large-scale data for protozoan and fungal pathogens, arthropod vectors, and their hosts, supporting >800 organisms and 2602 datasets across 12 component databases, OrthoMCL, and the newly added dataExplorer, as of Release 71 (August 2026). Since our last update, 292 datasets have been integrated, gene product descriptions improved, and OrthoMCL expanded to over 819 000 orthology groups spanning 9.2 million proteins. Artificial intelligence-assisted approaches now support dataset curation, community gene annotation, and experimental summaries of transcriptomic evidence on gene pages, each subject to expert or user review. The new My Datasets workspace lets researchers upload, analyze, and share their own data alongside curated datasets, and a guided interface supports differential expression analysis without programming. Infrastructure has been consolidated from 15 Oracle databases into a single PostgreSQL platform, with data-processing pipelines migrated to containerized Nextflow workflows. This period was also defined by the loss of the long-standing US federal award that funded VEuPathDB, its temporary closure in September 2024, and its restoration under a community-supported model of voluntary tiered subscriptions, donations, and philanthropic support, with all data and tools remaining freely accessible.

papers.title: Hypothalamic volume and cell-type changes in ageing and Alzheimer's disease.
papers.abstract: Alterations in metabolism, stress response, sleep, circadian rhythms and neuroendocrine processes are key features of ageing and neurodegeneration1,2. These fundamental processes are regulated by the hypothalamus, yet how its functionally distinct subregions and cell types change during human ageing and Alzheimer's disease (AD) remains largely unexplored. Here we present HypoAD, an atlas of the human hypothalamus in ageing and AD, including high-resolution magnetic resonance imaging from 458 individuals and single-nucleus RNA sequencing of 614,403 nuclei from young participants, patients with AD and age-matched non-dementia control participants. We show that hypothalamic subregions governing metabolism, stress and circadian rhythms are particularly vulnerable, showing notable changes in both volumes and gene expression during ageing and AD. At the molecular level, machine learning models identified the inflammatory response and regulators of circadian rhythms as key cellular predictors of AD. These signatures were reflected in specific cell types: microglia transitioned to a pro-inflammatory state, whereas inhibitory neurons within sleep-regulating and circadian-regulating hypothalamic subregions showed the most profound transcriptional alterations, including disruptions in ligand-receptor interactions and G-protein-coupled receptor signalling. HypoAD provides a high-resolution volumetric map and a transcriptomic atlas of the human hypothalamus in ageing and AD, relating lifestyle and behavioural changes to the relevant volumetric and molecular pathways. In addition, HypoAD provides a framework to investigate hypothalamic dysfunction and establishes a roadmap for targeted interventions aimed at mitigating physiological disruptions to potentially slow disease progression.

papers.title: De novo design of lipopeptides with antimicrobial potency enabled by a chain-as-prompt deep learning framework.
papers.abstract: Antimicrobial lipopeptides (AMLPs) represent a promising solution to global antibiotic crisis, yet their precision design remains challenging due to the inability of current computational models to account for N-terminal fatty acid modification. Here we develop a deep learning-driven AMLP model for de novo design of AMLPs by integrating a chain-as-prompt mechanism with domain-adaptive transfer learning, effectively bridging the representation gap between peptide sequence and lipid-induced bioactivity. Using the AMLP model, 2657 evolutionarily selected RiPP-derived core peptide sequences from 96,911 bacterial genomes are inspiringly designed for virtual lipidation with seven N-terminal fatty acid chains (C6-C18) followed by predictive screening, generating 6197 candidate sequences. Notably, we find that both high KRH rate ( ≥ 0.3) and common fatty acid tails (C12 and C16) are also critical for further selection of candidate AMLPs, resulting in 289 sequences. Then, 46 are randomly synthesized, with 44 showing antimicrobial activities (a positive rate of 95.7%). The lead antibiotic LP630 exhibits broad-spectrum activities against typical Gram-positive, Gram-negative and mycobacterial strains by targeting multiple bacterial cell membrane components, and demonstrates potent therapeutic efficacy in murine wound infection models. Our study provides a streamlined and universal paradigm for deep learning-enabled high-throughput discovery of novel lipopeptide therapeutics.

papers.title: Bacterial protein function prediction via multimodal deep learning.
papers.abstract: Bacterial proteins are specialized with extensive functional diversity for survival in diverse and stressful environments. A significant portion of these proteins remains functionally uncharacterized, limiting our understanding of bacterial survival mechanisms. Hence, we develop Deep Expression STructure (DeepEST), a multimodal deep learning framework that predicts protein function in bacteria by assigning Gene Ontology (GO) terms. DeepEST comprises two modules: a multi-layer perceptron that uses gene expression and gene location, and a protein structure-based module that uses predicted structures and amino acid sequences. Within DeepEST, we integrate these modules through a learnable weighted linear combination and introduce a novel masked loss function to fine-tune the structure-based predictor for bacterial species. These choices are well suited for bacteria, in which functionally related genes frequently colocalize and are cotranscribed within operons, allowing transcription dynamics to serve as informative, condition-dependent signals. We show that DeepEST outperforms existing protein function prediction methods on a 25-species benchmark, relying solely on amino acid sequence or protein structure. Averaged over the 25 species, DeepEST reaches a protein-centric F max of 0.689 and a term-centric micro-AUPRC of 0.756, a relative improvement of 4.4% and 11.6% over the second-best method, the structure-based predictor DeepFRI. Moreover, DeepEST predicts GO terms for unclassified hypothetical proteins across 25 human bacterial pathogens, supporting their experimental characterization. DeepEST bridges organism-specific data integration and structure-based transfer learning, providing a method tailored for bacterial protein function prediction in settings with structural and multi-condition expression data.

papers.title: Explainable AI identifies recombination and chromatin environment as key predictors of subgenome evolution in maize and Brassica.
papers.abstract: Polyploidy, or whole genome duplication, reshapes genomes through biased gene loss and regulatory rewiring, yet the drivers of biased fractionation among subgenomes remain unclear. Using maize and Brassica rapa as model allopolyploids, we compiled 60 genomic and epigenomic features in maize and 45 in B. rapa and constructed supervised machine learning models to classify genes by subgenome identity. In both species, eXplainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) approaches identified recombination rate as the most influential and highly interconnected feature despite nonsignificant mean differences between subgenome groups. Chromosome location, transposon density, and chromatin-associated features, including the proximity of accessible chromatin regions to genes and active histone marks such as H3K9ac and H3K27ac, consistently ranked among the top contributors to subgenome classification. XAI-derived covariation and interaction networks further revealed recombination rate as the central node connecting significant features. Together, these results highlight recombination and chromatin environment as major predictors of subgenome divergence in polyploid genomes.

papers.title: R-loopBase v2.0: species- and cell type-resolved quantitative R-loop maps and R-loop regulatory resources.
papers.abstract: R-loops are non-canonical nucleic acid structures implicated in diverse cellular processes and diseases. We previously developed R-loopBase to address the pressing challenges of inaccurate R-loop maps and the limited understanding of the R-loop regulatory network. However, R-loopBase provided only human R-loop maps with categorical confidence and did not account for cell type specificity. These limitations, coupled with the emerging R-loop profiling technologies and advances in R-loop regulatory mechanisms, have motivated the development of R-loopBase v2.0 (https://rloopbase.nju.edu.cn). After uniformly re-analysing 358 R-loop mapping datasets generated by 16 technologies, we introduce a quantitative R-loop scoring framework that assesses genome-wide R-loop confidence in human, demonstrating strong concordance with known R-loop biology. We further extend the framework to specific cell types and mouse, fruit fly, and yeast. In parallel, we substantially expand the collection of R-loop regulators across species, enabling the inference of changes in R-loop homeostasis. Building on these expanded datasets, we implement several new interactive features and analytical tools, including an expanded multi-species genome browser, deep learning-based R-loop prediction, R-loop homeostasis analysis, and a streamlined data download portal. We anticipate that R-loopBase v2.0 will serve as an enhanced, up-to-date one-stop resource for the R-loop research community.

papers.title: A framework for genome-wide characterization of DNA methylation and variant effect prediction.
papers.abstract: DNA methylation plays a critical role in many essential biological processes, including transcriptional regulation, genomic imprinting, chromosomal maintenance, genomic stability and development, and has phenotypic and disease impacts. However, genome-wide characterization of methylation patterns across cell types and tissues remains a major challenge. Here, to address this, we present a framework that enables systematic genome-wide analysis of methylation and sequence-based prediction of context-specific methylation effects of variants. Our data-driven discovery of methylation classes reveals context-dependent roles for methylation across tissues, cell types and regions of the genome. The framework also includes Wreath, a deep learning-based sequence model specifically designed to accurately predict the context-dependent impact of any genetic variant on methylation. These developments leverage a compendium that harmonizes disparate methylation profiles from disparate studies including over 90 tissues and cell types. Using Wreath, we systematically characterized the impact of noncoding pathogenic variants on tissue-specific methylation, generating mechanistic hypotheses for individual regulatory variants. We make the full framework, including the compendium, the methylation classes and the model, available for use by the community.

papers.title: Reconstructing the single-cell spatiotemporal dynamics of glioblastoma invasion.
papers.abstract: Glioblastoma invasion into healthy brain tissue remains a major barrier to effective treatment, but the dynamic single-cell behaviors underlying this process remain difficult to measure across patient models. Here, we introduce GlioTrace, an ex vivo imaging and computational framework for real-time tracking of glioblastoma invasion in patient-derived xenograft brain slices. Combining whole-specimen confocal microscopy with machine learning-based morphology classification and probabilistic modeling of state transitions, GlioTrace reconstructs how tumor cells switch between invasion phenotypes and how these dynamics are shaped by local tissue context and therapy. Across six patient-derived models, GlioTrace reveals that invasion plasticity is patient-specific, spatially organized, and modulated by vascular proximity and microglial interaction. Targeted therapies selectively alter phenotype composition and transition probabilities, whereas standard-of-care treatment enriches a highly motile, transition-connected branching state consistent with a treatment-tolerant invasive phenotype. Thus, GlioTrace makes glioblastoma invasion a measurable dynamic process for comparing patient-specific treatment responses in living brain tissue.

papers.title: Toward planetary microbial systems biology.
papers.abstract: Microorganisms underpin Earth's biosphere, sustaining life, shaping biogeochemical cycles, and maintaining ecosystem stability. In an era of scientific and geopolitical fragmentation, we advocate for a "planetary microbial systems biology" (PMSB) framework to uncover the mechanisms and organizational principles governing Earth's interconnected microbial systems across scales of matter, space, and time and in relation to underlying natural and anthropogenic drivers. PMSB combines molecular and cellular technologies, multi-omics data, artificial intelligence (AI), and integrated transdisciplinary research across ecosystems. By federating open data and combining field observations, experimentation, and modeling, PMSB enables predictive understanding of microbiome dynamics across planetary scales, thus filling a critical knowledge gap in our understanding of the co-evolution of life and the Earth-system.

papers.title: Deciphering the limitations of immortalized hepatocyte cell lines for the study of liver cis-regulatory elements
papers.abstract: Background: Immortalized cell lines are widely used to study transcriptional regulation. However, previous studies have shown that immortalization and prolonged culture can alter their regulatory landscapes, potentially compromising their ability to model native cis-regulatory element (CRE) activity. Hepatocyte-like cell lines (HLCs), particularly HepG2, are frequently used to study liver CREs, but whether non-cancer-derived HLCs, such as AML12, better recapitulate native regulatory landscapes remains unclear. Furthermore, cell culture conditions have been shown to influence gene expression and CRE activity, raising the possibility that optimizing culture conditions could improve HLC gene regulatory similarities to primary liver tissue. Together, these questions highlight the importance of characterizing the transcriptional regulatory landscapes of HLCs and evaluating the effects of culture conditions when using these cell lines to study native liver CRE activity. Results: We systematically characterized the molecular features and transcriptional regulatory landscapes of four HLCs and compared them with those of liver tissue. We examined AML12 cells using RT-qPCR and flow cytometry and found that they express some hepatocyte markers but lack key characteristics of mature hepatocytes. We then used ATAC-seq to characterize the chromatin accessibility landscape of AML12. Through transcription factor motif enrichment, functional enrichment, and machine learning analyses, we found substantial differences in the cis-regulatory landscapes of AML12 and primary mouse liver. Modifying AML12 culture conditions altered some regulatory features but did not substantially improve their similarity to primary liver tissue. We then extended these analyses to three additional HLCs and found similar differences between their regulatory landscapes and that of primary liver tissue. Notably, HepG2 recapitulated native liver regulatory landscapes better than the tested non-cancer-derived cell lines. Conclusion: Our findings reveal substantial differences in transcriptional regulatory landscapes between immortalized HLCs and native liver tissue that persist despite modifications to culture conditions. These results highlight the limitations of HLCs in modeling native liver transcriptional regulation and emphasize the importance of evaluating their regulatory landscapes before using them to investigate CRE function. Keywords: Hepatocyte-like cell lines; Cis-regulatory elements; Liver; Cell culture conditions; ATAC-seq

papers.title: SpliceVarMech: A causal generative framework for mechanistic interpretation of non-canonical splicing variants
papers.abstract: Non-canonical splicing variants occur beyond the conserved dinucleotides flanking splice junctions and are difficult to interpret because disruption scores alone do not explain splice outcomes or quantify uncertainty. We have developed SpliceVarMech, a causal generative framework in which a dual-stream encoder compares the wild-type and mutant sequences and conditional discrete sequence diffusion generates candidate splice outcomes. We then apply Bayesian causal inference to estimate posterior disruption probabilities with 95% credible intervals. The framework reports the predicted splice mechanism together with sequence attribution maps and an exploratory mapping to clinical evidence labels. On a gold-standard cohort of experimentally validated variants from male infertility genes, Bayesian leave-one-out cross-validation on 31 variants yielded an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 1.000. We benchmarked 16 individual splice prediction tools on the same cohort, where the highest-performing tool, SpliceAI, achieved 0.619 on its 30 scored variants. Ablation experiments showed that removing individual components reduced discrimination, and a separate evaluation on 54 variants supported the contribution of fine-tuning. In a cross-domain assessment, fine-tuning on BRCA1 saturation genome editing data increased discrimination from 0.722 to 0.840 on 203 held-out variants without architectural modification. We assessed in-sample calibration, and held-out validation remains necessary. These results support further evaluation of paired-sequence generative modeling and Bayesian inference for mechanistic interpretation of splicing variants across disease contexts.

papers.title: Genomic foundation models and complementary variant-scoring strategies in LGMD-associated genes: architecture, adaptation, and sequence context
papers.abstract: Genomic foundation models learn representations from DNA sequence, although their usefulness for variant classification depends on the architecture and downstream evaluation procedure. We compared six genomic foundation models using 6,960 ClinVar single-nucleotide variants from ten limb-girdle muscular dystrophy (LGMD)-associated genes, with 4,866 variants assigned to training and 2,094 to held-out testing. The analyses included frozen alternate-minus-reference embeddings at 101, 201 and 501 bp, supervised adaptation at 101 bp, and gene-held-out downstream classifier training. GPN-Star V100 and AlphaGenome Atlas AVI were evaluated separately using their native scores. At 101 bp, frozen Evo2 achieved the highest discrimination among the six foundation models (MCC 0.644; AUROC 0.879; AUPRC 0.818). Supervised adaptation increased MCC for three architectures and reduced it for the remaining three. Extending sequence context to 501 bp improved all three primary metrics in five of six frozen architectures, with Evo2 reaching an MCC of 0.864, AUROC of 0.964 and AUPRC of 0.952. Evo2 also led the frozen gene-held-out readouts (pooled MCC 0.641; AUROC 0.852; AUPRC 0.789). GPN-Star V100 and AVI achieved MCC values of 0.929 and 0.938, respectively, using distinct biological inputs and scoring procedures. The number of variants misclassified across all evaluated configurations decreased from five under the original 101-bp readouts to one after including longer contexts and native scores. An exploratory HGVS-category control identified substantial annotation-associated structure in the benchmark labels. The findings characterize classification performance against aggregate ClinVar labels within LGMD-associated genes. Disease-specific pathogenicity and clinical diagnostic utility remain untested.

papers.title: SteMClass: A DNA Methylation-Based Classifier for iPSC In Vitro Differentiation States.
papers.abstract: Human induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) hold great promise for regenerative medicine, disease modelling, and drug discovery, but most downstream applications require differentiation into specialised cell types not covered by current quality control assays. Here, we present SteMClass, a prototype DNA methylation-based classifier that standardises iPSC differentiation state identification across protocols with one test. We curated a reference cohort of 15 iPSC lines differentiated into seven distinct states (n = 97), performed array-based DNA methylation profiling, and trained a random forest model to classify the eight distinct differentiation states. In nested cross-validation, SteMClass achieved a Brier score of 0.018, and on an independent cohort (n = 58) attained 96.5% accuracy (Cohens K = 0.959) with a 3% rejection rate. Applied to external data (n = 249), SteMClass achieved 85.1% overall accuracy (Cohens K = 0.687) with a 12.9% rejection rate. Among classified samples (n = 217), accuracy was 97.7% (Cohens K = 0.93). SteMClass is compatible with all Illumina methylation array versions, and accessible via an interactive web interface that supports classification and exploration of DNA methylation profiles. By providing a harmonised, single-assay framework for iPSC-derived differentiation state characterisation, SteMClass improves reproducibility and comparability across studies, paving the way for robust quality control standards and accelerating clinical translation.

papers.title: BRIDGE: inter-tissue imputation with contrastive learning improves recovery of donor-specific gene expression
papers.abstract: Multi-tissue transcriptome resources are central to understanding tissue-specific regulation and inter-individual variation. Realistically, most tissues are measured in only a subset of donors, especially for less accessible tissues such as brain and heart. Accurately imputing gene expression values for such tissues, while accounting for individual heterogeneity, remains a daunting challenge. Here, we present BRIDGE (Body-wide Representation via Inter-tissue Decoding of Gene Expression), a lightweight framework that imputes donor-specific and tissue-specific expression measures using contrastive learning. When tested on real-world expression data from the Genotype-Tissue Expression (GTEx) consortium, BRIDGE recovered donor-specific variation more accurately than existing state-of-the-art methods while improving overall accuracy, with the largest advantage found in the most inaccessible tissues. We provide the BRIDGE-imputed completed GTEx v11 donor x tissue xgene expression tensor as a resource to the broader research community.

papers.title: VenusPheno: Transfer-Guided Task Grouping for Multi-Task Bacterial Phenotype Prediction
papers.abstract: Understanding how genomic information gives rise to bacterial phenotypes is a fundamental problem in biology. Genome-level prediction requires models that integrate information from thousands of proteins, while related phenotypes may share genomic signals. However, not all phenotype tasks benefit from being learned together, and suitable task groups can be difficult to define from biological knowledge alone. We present VenusPheno, a framework that combines multiple-instance learning over pretrained ProtT5 protein embeddings with transfer-guided multi-task learning. An attention-based Set Transformer aggregates the proteins in each genome into a genome-level representation. We evaluate VenusPheno on 14 binary phenotype tasks from 12,178 bacterial genomes using genus-disjoint splits. Under single-task training, VenusPheno outperforms computational, conventional machine-learning, and deep-learning baselines in terms of mean balanced accuracy. We then use leave-one-task-out analysis to estimate directed transfer relationship between phenotypes, revealing both beneficial and detrimental interactions. Grouping tasks based on these transfer relationships further improves mean balanced accuracy over independent training and joint training of all tasks. Although inferred without biological priors, the resulting groups are consistent with biologically plausible relationships among phenotypes. VenusPheno therefore combines accurate phenotype prediction with a data-driven strategy for determining which tasks should be learned together. The PyTorch implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/YJinling/VenusPheno.

papers.title: RIPPLE: learning nucleotide relations in an RNA foundation model
papers.abstract: RNA function depends on interactions between nucleotides that can be widely separated in sequence, yet capturing these relationships remains challenging for RNA language models. Existing approaches primarily learn nucleotide relationships implicitly from individual nucleotide reconstruction or rely on external structural information to model nucleotide interactions. Here we introduce RIPPLE, an RNA foundation model that learns to identify and represent sparse, predictively useful nucleotide relationships directly from sequence. Pretrained on 32.4 million RNA sequences, RIPPLE uses pairwise predictive utility to guide relational learning, transferring training-time supervision into a sequence-only model without requiring structural inputs at inference. RIPPLE improves overall performance across five downstream tasks spanning RNA family classification, ribosome loading prediction, secondary-structure prediction, three-dimensional contact prediction, and splice-site recognition. Mechanistic analyses further show that utility-guided learning improves the recovery of informative interactions and enhances the transferability of learned RNA representations.

papers.title: HapAdapter: A Transfer Learning Protocol for DNA Foundation Models Adapted to Diploid Personal Epigenomes
papers.abstract: The rapid rise of large language models (LLMs) has spurred the development of genomic language models (gLMs) that capitalize on the key features of natural language present in biological sequences. Moreover, DNA foundation models, a sub-class of gLMs, have demonstrated impressive accuracy in predicting a wide range of functional tracks from DNA sequence input. However, current DNA foundation models are exclusively trained on haploid reference genome sequences -- despite personal and graph genomes becoming the new standard for genomic analyses. This is principally because the cost to train gLMs on a personal diploid genome for a single individual is not currently practical. To help reconcile this disconnect between the current available use-cases of DNA foundation models with the modern direction of genomic sequence analysis, we present HapAdapter, a transfer-learning protocol that builds a small Siamese network on top of any pre-trained foundation model to enable inference from full diploid personal genome context. To demonstrate the utility of this method, we train a set of HapAdapter heads to predict allele-specific effects across assays on two representative foundation model backbones: DNABERT-2 and AlphaGenome. We demonstrate that our lightweight adapter more than doubles DNABERT-2's allele-specific discrimination and triples AlphaGenome's (130% and 210% gain in AUROC above chance, respectively, averaged over nine assays).

papers.title: VS-Suite: Automated Consensus Virtual Screening Platform for Improved Screening of Small Molecules
papers.abstract: Growing the recent advances in artificial intelligence and machine leaning (AI&ML) approaches accelerated small molecules screening against targeted proteins with limited computational resources and time. Finding accurate binding pose and affinity prediction is challenges task and traditional docking tools and lacks the reproducibility. Development of the Co-folding model is paradigm shift in drug discovery and development, allowing to predict protein ligand complexes without experimental crystal structures. Notably Boltz-2 predicts the complex structure along with binding affinity directly using protein FASTA sequence and ligand SMILES. Our previous studies confirmed that Boltz-2 is classify binder non-binders effectively. Autodock Vina and GNINA are widely used docking with knowledge and CNN based scoring functions allows to screen potential small molecules. We developed in-house VS-suite (Virtual Screening Suite) multi-environment conda orchestration designed to automate the docking workflow only using FASTA and SMILES string as inputs via streamlit-based browser GUI which integrates the boltz-2 for the complex structure prediction followed docking using AutoDock Vina for Gnina. Validation on 58 antiviral nucleoside analogues screened against SARS-CoV-2 main protease (Mpro). VS-Suite is available at https://github.com/Vsubuchem-lab/Virtual-screening-suite-VS-Suite. This consensus approaches helpful in rapid screening of small molecules against selected targets. The findings and VS-suite support its utility as a rapid and reliable tool for hit identification and rational drug development.

papers.title: Is the Bitter Lesson coming to genomic prediction? An untuned tabular foundation model matches or beats specialized methods
papers.abstract: Genomic prediction (GP) is dominated by models designed around assumptions about how genetic variation affects phenotypes. Here we asked how well a general-purpose pretrained tabular foundation model called TabPFN-3.5 does with no genetics-specific modeling and no tuning when given marker genotypes directly. We benchmarked TabPFN-3.5 using a published comparison of 18 GP methods on 18 traits in six plant species. TabPFN-3.5 ranked first on 11 of 18 traits and had the best median rank among all methods. Because the published benchmark did not identify its test sets, we reran GBLUP, RKHS and elastic-net models on the same splits as TabPFN-3.5. Against the best of these, TabPFN-3.5 was ahead on 12 of 18 traits, with significant gains on all three soybean traits and rice flowering time. In the soybean panel, which had the largest number of lines, its advantage was clearest. In leave-families-out cross-validation, where models were trained on some soybean families and used to predict lines from other families withheld from training, every model lost accuracy and TabPFN-3.5 performed on par with GBLUP and RKHS. Our results show that a general-purpose learner matches or exceeds decades of specialized GP models. This finding is consistent with Sutton's ``Bitter Lesson'', which holds that methods that scale with computation eventually overtake those built on human knowledge of the domain.

papers.title: MINet: a microbiome foundation model integrating microbial co-occurrence priors with abundance information
papers.abstract: The composition and dynamics of microbial communities are shaped by complex ecological interactions among taxa, yet most existing microbiome foundation models rely largely on the categorical identity of microbial taxa, giving limited attention to the association structure and quantitative abundance within communities. Here we present Microbial Interaction Network (MINet), a microbiome foundation model that integrates microbial co-occurrence priors with an abundance-aware mechanism. Specifically, we construct a large-scale microbial co-occurrence network from the standardized data of the Earth Microbiome Project (EMP) to provide co-occurrence-based association priors for the model, and then pretrain MINet autoregressively on more than 260,000 microbiome samples (MicroCorpus-260K). In addition to standard attention, MINet encodes z-score-normalized abundance values as input features through a two-layer multilayer perceptron, and superimposes a co-occurrence bias matrix onto the attention scores with a learnable weight, so that the attention distribution reflects both the sequence context and interactions among microorganisms. Our results show that (i) the full model consistently outperforms ablated variants with the co-occurrence bias or abundance removed in terms of pretraining loss; (ii) on the task of predicting naphthalene degradation rates for 14-strain synthetic consortia, the Transformer architecture with abundance learning significantly outperforms the vanilla Transformer and conventional machine learning methods; (iii) on downstream tasks such as biome classification and prediction of infant gut microbiota developmental stages, MINet achieves performance comparable to or better than MGM; and (iv) in generation tasks trained on data from different environments, MINet produces ecologically plausible synthetic communities whose diversity, compositional structure and co-occurrence patterns closely match those of real communities. These findings demonstrate that explicitly incorporating microbial co-occurrence priors and abundance information into pretraining can effectively enhance the representational capacity and ecological plausibility of microbiome foundation models, providing a new modelling paradigm for community-scale microbiome analysis.

papers.title: Adapting Echocardiographic Foundation Models for Detecting Pulmonary Embolism-Related Right-Heart Strain
papers.abstract: Pulmonary embolism (PE) is a time-sensitive medical emergency in which rapid recognition of right ventricular (RV) dysfunction by point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) can support early risk stratification. Here, we present HOPE (ecHO-Pulmonary Embolism), a real-world emergency cardiac POCUS video dataset comprising 4,069 patients with suspected PE, and EchoPE1, a foundation-model-based video classification framework for detecting PE-associated right-heart phenotypes. HOPE includes five commonly acquired emergency echocardiographic views, with all positive PE cases confirmed by computed tomography pulmonary angiography. EchoPE builds on EchoPrime-pretrained echocardiographic representations and incorporates view recognition, task-specific adaptation, and attention-based interpretability. Experiments suggested that directly transferring EchoPrime representations to this disease-specific task provided limited performance, whereas EchoPE (AUROC 95.2 {+/-} .3) substantially outperformed both EchoPrime with a classification head (AUROC 87.6 {+/-} 1) and conventional video deep learning baselines. At a fixed sensitivity of 90%, EchoPE achieved a precision of 87.8, compared with 70.7 for EchoPrime. Among adaptation strategies, Low-Rank Adaptation combined with knowledge distillation provided the best balance between PE discrimination and preservation of pretrained echocardiographic semantics. Interpretability analyses showed that the adapted model focused on clinically relevant RV morphological changes, interventricular septal configuration, and informative temporal segments within ultrasound videos. Overall, HOPE and EchoPE demonstrate that echocardiographic foundation models require dataset-specific adaptation to identify PE-related right-heart strain and support the potential use of artificial intelligence-assisted bedside echocardiography for risk warning in acute care settings.

papers.title: From Sequence Uncertainty to Phenotype Hypotheses: Uncertainty-Conditioned Inference over Biomedical Knowledge Graphs
papers.abstract: Genomic foundation models provide variant-level evidence, but connecting that evidence to phenotype hypotheses requires accounting for uncertainty throughout structured reasoning. We introduce an uncertainty-conditioned path-energy framework that converts sequence predictions and calibrated predictive uncertainty into explicit distributions over graph-supported phenotype hypotheses, without patient-level phenotype supervision. An interpretable learned energy scores admissible gene--disease--phenotype routes, query uncertainty controls the target temperature, and path probabilities are aggregated into phenotype hypotheses. This formulation makes evidence quality an explicit determinant of hypothesis breadth while retaining traceable multi-path support. Exact normalization over enumerable candidate sets provides a reference for evaluating a Hastings-corrected learned revision operator. On AlzKB and Hetionet, phenotype-level entropy tracks upstream uncertainty, with Spearman correlations of 0.951 and 0.878, respectively; ablations identify the contribution of uncertainty conditioning. In masked-edge recovery, the model exceeds chance and degree-matched probability-permutation controls. Training the energy under the uncertainty-dependent temperature yields higher held-out recall@10 than training under a constant temperature of comparable magnitude. Under gene hold-out, recall@10 exceeds that of a trained DistMult embedding on 24 of 30 graph masks (0.183 versus 0.123); this difference is attributable mainly to three genes with many variants and is not established for all genes. These results establish an uncertainty-aware interface from genomic predictions to graph-supported phenotype hypotheses that combines interpretable probability allocation with held-out association recovery of explicitly stated scope.

papers.title: STORM: A Lightweight Structure-Free Model for Binding Affinity Prediction
papers.abstract: Accurately predicting a small molecule's binding affinity to a protein, a critical task in drug discovery, remains challenging.
